content.text:
All five core files are written, tested and committed, one commit each, and `make check` passes. Below is every function in plain language. Read this closely: these are the files the live session will dig into.

---

## 1. BM25 search: [internal/retrieve/bm25.go](internal/retrieve/bm25.go)
**The job:** given a question, find the chunks of the papers most likely to contain the answer.

- **`k1` and `b`** are two tuning numbers:
  - `k1 = 1.2`: a word appearing 10 times in a chunk isn't 10× as relevant as appearing once. Extra repeats count less and less.
  - `b = 0.75`: long chunks contain more words, so they match more by chance. This number penalises length.
- **`Hit`** is one search result: the chunk plus two scores.
  - `Score` is the raw BM25 score, used only to rank results within one search.
  - `Norm` is the score as a fraction of the best possible score for that question, between 0 and 1. The "should I refuse?" threshold T uses this one.
- **`NewIndex`** reads every chunk once, up front, like building the index at the back of a book. For each chunk it records which words appear and how often, and how long the chunk is. It also records, for each word, how many chunks contain it. All of this happens once, so searching is fast.
- **`idf`** measures how rare a word is. A word like "model" is in almost every chunk, so it says little. "WavLM" is in a few, so a match on it says a lot. Rare words get bigger weights.
- **`Search`**:
  1. Splits the question into words, each counted once.
  2. Works out the best score this question could possibly get.
  3. Scores every chunk and drops those scoring 0.
  4. Sorts best-first. When two chunks tie, it keeps their original order, so every run gives the same result.
  5. Returns the top k.
- **`score`** is the BM25 formula for one chunk. For each question word in the chunk, it adds (how rare the word is) × (how often it appears, with diminishing returns) ÷ (an adjustment for chunk length).
- **`unique`**: asking "attention attention" is the same question as asking "attention".

**Why `Norm` matters (D10):** "speech model" and "speech dijkstra" give nearly the same raw score on the speech chunk (1.24 vs 1.09). Normalised, they're 0.51 vs 0.16, because the papers never mention Dijkstra. That gap is what lets the system refuse off-topic questions.

## 2. Verify: [internal/pipeline/verify.go](internal/pipeline/verify.go)
**The job:** check the model's draft using simple text checks before anyone sees it. This is how "never wrong" is enforced.

- **`RefusalText`** is the exact sentence the model must use when the papers don't answer: "The papers do not say."
- **`Verdict`** is the result:
  - whether the draft passed
  - whether it was a refusal
  - which chunks it cited
  - a list of problems, written so they can be pasted straight into the "please redraft" prompt
- **`Verify`** runs these checks in order:
  1. Is the draft empty? That fails. (The probe showed Groq can return an empty answer.)
  2. Is it a refusal? Accept it.
  3. Does it cite at least one chunk, and was every cited chunk actually given to the model? An invented ID like `[…#99]` fails.
  4. For every quote, find the citation right after it. Is the quoted text in that chunk, word for word? A real quote attributed to the wrong chunk fails.
  5. Is there at least one quote of 3 or more words? A citation with no quote isn't enough evidence (D11).
- **`isRefusal`** spots the refusal sentence at the start, ignoring capitals and spacing. Only the refusal sentence is shown, never anything after it, because the rest is unchecked.
- **`group`** picks out the quoted text, whether the model used straight quotes `"…"` or curly ones `“…”`.
- **`citationAfter`** finds which citation a quote belongs to: the first one after it.
- **`normalize`** removes differences that don't matter: extra spaces, curly versus straight apostrophes, different dash characters. Capital letters still have to match exactly.
- **`trimEnd`** ignores a full stop the writer put inside the closing quote mark.

**Known limit (a test pins it down):** a correct quote placed next to a false claim still passes.

## 3. Limiter: [internal/traffic/limiter.go](internal/traffic/limiter.go)
**The job:** our own count of how much of Groq's allowance is left, so we stay under its limits rather than relying on Groq to stop us. The probe showed Groq let 34 calls through a 30-per-minute limit.

- **`Limits` / `GroqFree`** hold the measured limits: 30 requests/minute, 8,000 tokens/minute, 1,000 requests/day, and 200,000 tokens/day (that last one from the docs only).
- **`ByMinute`, `ByDay`, `ByPause`** say *why* a request has to wait. The difference matters: a minute limit means "wait a bit or give a smaller answer"; a day limit means "the budget is gone".
- **`NewLimiter`** creates four token buckets, all full. Think of each as a tank that refills at a steady rate (D6).
- **`Wait`** asks "how long until these requests and tokens would fit?" without taking anything. Admission uses it to estimate how long a queue will take.
- **`Fits`** asks whether this single request could *ever* fit. A 9,000-token request never fits an 8,000-token-per-minute limit.
- **`wait`** checks all four tanks plus any active pause, and returns the longest wait along with its reason.
- **`TryReserve`** takes room for one call if there's room right now. It reserves "prompt + maximum output", deliberately too much, to be safe.
- **`Reservation.Finish`** runs once Groq reports the real token count. Unused tokens go back in the tank; if the call used more than reserved, the extra is charged.
- **`Reservation.Cancel`** runs when the call was never sent, and returns everything. Calling Finish or Cancel twice does nothing the second time, so nothing is refunded twice.
- **`Observe`** uses Groq's headers to correct our count, but only downward. Inside a burst, the headers contradicted each other, so believing the lowest number is the safe choice.
- **`PauseFor`** applies when Groq says "429, retry after N seconds": nobody starts a new call for N seconds. A later, shorter pause can't cut that short.

## 4. Retry: [internal/traffic/retry.go](internal/traffic/retry.go)
**The job:** decide whether a failed call is worth trying again, and how long to wait first.

- **`Policy`** holds the settings:
  - the maximum number of retries
  - the first wait and the largest wait
  - whether to add randomness to waits
  - whether to follow Groq's "retry after" hint
  - the minimum time an attempt needs
  - test hooks for a fake clock and randomness
- **`DefaultPolicy`** is the real policy:
  - 2 retries at most
  - waits start at 500ms and are capped at 8s
  - waits include randomness
  - Groq's hint is followed
  - an attempt needs at least 250ms, about the fastest answer the probe saw
- **`NaivePolicy`** is deliberately bad: a fixed 1-second wait, no randomness, Groq's hint ignored. It exists for the required "retrying made things worse" run.
- **`Retryable`** decides whether to retry at all. Yes for "too many requests", server errors, timeouts and dropped connections, because those can clear up on their own. No for other 4xx errors, which mean our request is wrong and will fail again, and no if the caller has already given up.
- **`Delay`** decides how long to wait:
  - If Groq gave a hint, wait that long plus a small random extra. Without the extra, everyone told "2 seconds" comes back at the same instant and causes the same pile-up again.
  - Otherwise wait 0.5s, then 1s, then 2s and so on, capped at 8s, and pick a random point between zero and that number.
- **`Stats`** records how many retries happened, how many 429s were seen, and how long was spent waiting. All three go into `results.csv`.
- **`Do`** runs the call and retries per the policy. It stops on success, on an error not worth retrying, when retries run out, or when waiting plus another attempt would finish after the person's deadline. An answer that arrives after the person gave up is worth nothing.

## 5. Admission: [internal/traffic/admission.go](internal/traffic/admission.go)
**The job:** when a request arrives, decide what the person gets, and make them wait their turn.

- **`Level` (L0–L3)** is the ladder:
  - L0: full answer
  - L1: lighter answer, with fewer chunks and no redraft
  - L2: "busy, try again in N seconds"
  - L3: daily budget gone, so show the relevant passages from the papers with citations and make no model call
- **`AdmissionConfig`** has two settings: the maximum queue length, and the expected time a model call takes once it starts.
- **`Decision`** records the chosen level, the "try again in N" value for L2, the estimated wait, the queue length on arrival, and the reason. These go into the results.
- **`NewAdmission` / `Close`** start and stop the background worker that serves the queue.
- **`Decide`** picks the level:
  1. Estimate the wait for *this request plus everyone already queued ahead of it*. That estimate comes from the limiter.
  2. If the daily limit is the blocker → **L3**.
  3. If the queue is full → **L2**.
  4. If the full answer would finish before the person gives up → **L0**.
  5. If only the lighter answer would → **L1**.
  6. Otherwise → **L2**, with N taken from the limiter.

  It never queues someone who would only time out in the queue.
- **`Acquire`** joins the back of the line and waits for room. If the person gives up while waiting, they leave the line at that moment, so they don't hold up anyone behind them. If room was granted at the exact moment they gave up, it's handed back.
- **`dispatch`** is the background worker. It looks at whoever is first in line and asks the limiter for room. If there's room, that request goes. If not, it sleeps exactly as long as the limiter says, waking early if the line changes.
- **`leave`** removes a request from the line. **`wake`** nudges the worker. **`QueueLen`** reports how many are waiting.

---

## Three bugs caught along the way
1. **The limiter's wait came out 1ns short.** 1000 ÷ 133.33 in floating point gives 7.4999999s, so a sleeper would wake a hair too early and loop again. Waits now round **up**.
2. **A long queue was treated as "never fits".** The queue-wide wait estimate passed the total through the same "is it bigger than the tank?" check used for one request. Six requests of 2,000 tokens add up to more than the 8K tank, so `Decide` would have given **L3, budget gone**, to people who only needed to wait. Queue estimates now use a separate calculation without that check (D12). A test now covers it.
3. **My own first draft of the admission tests was broken.** One test was a leftover stub, and another held the lock and never called `Decide`. I caught both before running anything, and rewrote them as real tests. Fixing them is what exposed bug 2.

**One gap left for the pipeline wiring:** after a 429, the code that wires everything together must call `limiter.Observe(…)` and `limiter.PauseFor(retry-after)`. The retry policy can't do it, because it knows nothing about the limiter. That's the main job of Phase 5, along with the rewrite step, the prompt, and the L3 retrieval-only reply.

content.text:
Phase 5 is the wiring. **Rewrite → retrieve → decide → admission → draft (with retries) → verify (with at most one redraft) → reply.** It needs four files:

- `rewrite.go`: drop question filler words.
- `prompt.go`: the model's rules, and the `[id] text` chunk format the stand-in already expects.
- `pipeline.go`: `Answer`, the one function that uses all five core files.
- `cmd/relay`: a command-line tool for asking a single question.

Two choices to flag now:

1. **What status do L2 and L3 get in `results.csv`?** Both are recorded as `rate_limited`, with `ladder_level` telling them apart. An L3 reply is useful, but it isn't a model answer, and a limit is the reason. Calling it `ok` would make the "budget exhausted" row of Table 2b look perfect when it isn't.
2. **What counts as "first token" for the person?** The reply is held back until it passes verify (DESIGN §2), so the first token the person sees arrives with the full reply. I record the model's own first token separately, for the "where the time goes" heading.

The pipeline is built and committed (`fcb79d0`), and it works end to end on real Groq.

## Real results
| Question | What happened | Time | Tokens |
|---|---|---|---|
| Why does the Transformer scale dot products? | Verified on draft 2: 3 uncited sentences dropped, 2 exact quotes kept, citations shown as `[1706.03762v7, §3.2.1, p.4]` | 1.8s | 3,447 / 378 |
| Dijkstra's time complexity | Retrieval scored 0.139, below T = 0.2: "The papers do not say." | 0ms | 0 |

## The new files, in plain language
**[rewrite.go](internal/pipeline/rewrite.go)**
- `Rewrite` turns a question into a search query. It strips words that only frame the question ("can you please explain…") and keeps the meaningful ones, including numbers and technical terms.

**[prompt.go](internal/pipeline/prompt.go)**
- The system prompt states the same rules verify checks, plus a format example that uses a made-up chunk ID.
- `Messages` builds the request with one `[id] text` line per chunk.
- `Redraft` adds "your answer failed these checks: …" so the model's second try knows exactly what was wrong.
- `estimateTokens` is a rough token count calibrated from the probe: 72 tokens of overhead plus one per 5 characters.

**[pipeline.go](internal/pipeline/pipeline.go)**
- `Settings` hold R1, R2 and R3.
- `Answer` runs the five steps:
  1. Search.
  2. If the best match is weak, refuse without calling the model.
  3. Ask admission for a ladder rung.
  4. Draft, drop uncited sentences, then verify.
  5. Redraft once at L0; at L1, refuse instead.
- `draft` makes one model call. Each attempt, retries included, waits in the queue and holds a limiter reservation.
- `settle` updates the limiter after each call: it settles the reservation, corrects counts from the headers, and on a 429 pauses everyone.
- `statusOf` maps the final error to the brief's status values.
- `renderCitations` turns `[1706.03762v7#9]` into `[1706.03762v7, §3.2.1, p.4]`.
- `busy` writes the L2 reply.
- `passages` writes the L3 reply: the top 3 matching excerpts, cited, with no model call.

**[cmd/relay](cmd/relay/main.go)** asks one question from the command line, against Groq or the stand-in, and prints the timing breakdown.

## Problems found while building, all fixed with regression tests
1. **A failed call emptied the daily budget.** A response with no headers carried zero-value limits, which the limiter read as "0 requests left today". After one dropped connection, everyone would have got L3. I caught it because a test took 10 seconds instead of milliseconds.
2. **Verify let an unsupported sentence through. That was my mistake in core file 2.** The first real answer included a sentence from the model's own knowledge, and it passed because verify only required one good quote somewhere. Every sentence now needs a citation. Uncited sentences are **dropped**, not the whole answer refused: the person gets less, never an unbacked claim.
3. **Verify refused correct quotes.** The model lowercased a quote's first word and joined two passages with "…". Both are normal quoting habits. Each piece is now checked separately, ignoring case.

Problems 2 and 3 work well for the "How I worked with the assistant" section: something it got wrong, caught by checking real output rather than trusting passing tests. I tuned verify on only three real answers, so the eval will show whether the false-refusal rate is acceptable.

**Groq usage today:** about 74 of 1,000 requests. That leaves plenty for 3 settings × 20 questions plus a small real steady run.

content.text:
Phase 8 is the load generator. Here's the plan, following DESIGN §6:

- **Open loop.** Requests start at their scheduled times whether or not earlier ones have finished. Latency is measured from the scheduled start, so a slow system can't hide behind a slow generator.
- **Lag check.** Every row records how late its start actually was (good-to-have #2).
- **Scenarios** are defined in code: arrival rates, how the stand-in behaves, what our limiter believes, and which retry policy is used.
- **Eval mode** runs the questions one at a time and grades each answer.

Two scenario decisions, both driven by the probe:

1. **Rates are set by TPM, not RPM.** At about 1.9K tokens per answer, 8K TPM allows roughly **4 answers a minute**. So "steady" means 3 per minute, and "overload" means 12 per minute (3× capacity).
2. **"Per-minute limit halved" halves the *provider* without telling our limiter.** The brief says limits "can change without notice". Our limiter still believes 8K TPM, and only learns the truth from Groq's headers and 429s. That's also where the naive retry policy can do real damage, which makes the comparison meaningful.

cat >> DECISIONS.md <<'EOF'

## D14 — 2026-11-12 — Load generator and scenarios

**Decisions:**
- Arrivals are a seeded Poisson process per phase (exponential gaps), not evenly spaced: real traffic is bursty even at a steady average. Bursts are N requests at one instant.
- Open loop: each request starts at its scheduled time in its own goroutine; latency runs from the scheduled start; every row records `start_lag_ms` (good-to-have #2, an extra column after the brief's).
- Rates follow the probe: TPM binds at ~4 answers/minute, so steady = 3/min, overload = 12/min. Burst = steady plus 20 at once at 1:00. "Halved" halves the stand-in's RPM/TPM *without telling our limiter*, which must learn from headers and 429s. "Daily-exhausted" starts the stand-in's RPD at 0 with the 86.4 s trickle.
- The naive-retry run is any scenario with `-policy naive`, so the comparison holds arrivals, seed and provider fixed. The naive policy also skips the limiter-wide pause on a 429 (otherwise our limiter would quietly make it polite).
- Eval runs the questions closed loop, one at a time, so Table 3 latencies are the pipeline's, not a queue's. Grading: every key phrase present and a citation from the expected paper.
- Only `eval` and `steady` may run against real Groq; the rest are refused on `-source real` to protect the shared daily budget.
- First token for timeouts/errors is empty: the person saw no answer.

**Cost:** Patience is a fixed 20 s for everyone (a guess, DESIGN §5); the runs show what it costs. Stand-in answer grades are meaningless (D9).
EOF
make check 2>&1 | grep -E 'FAIL|gofmt needed|^ok.*(loadgen|eval|results|pipeline)' ; git add -A DECISIONS.md cmd/loadgen internal/loadgen internal/eval internal/results internal/pipeline && git commit -q -m "Add open-loop load generator, scenarios and grading

Seeded Poisson arrivals, each request started on schedule in its own
goroutine, latency from the scheduled start, start lag recorded per
row. Scenarios: steady, burst, overload, halved (provider limits
change without notice), daily-exhausted, and -policy naive for the
retry comparison. Eval mode answers each question once and grades it.
Real Groq is allowed only for eval and steady." && git log --oneline | head -1

lines: - Quotes are compared case-insensitively, and a quote joining passages with "…" is checked piece by piece. Real Groq answers lowercased a quote's first word and joined two passages with an ellipsis; both are normal quoting and do not change what the source says.

**Cost:** Dropping sentences can leave a terse answer of quotes. Case-insensitive matching is slightly looser than "word for word". These were tuned on three real answers; the eval measures the false-refusal rate properly.
+- Arrivals are a seeded Poisson process per phase (exponential gaps), not evenly spaced: real traffic is bursty even at a steady average. Bursts are N requests at one instant.

+- Open loop: each request starts at its scheduled time in its own goroutine; latency runs from the scheduled start; every row records `start_lag_ms` (good-to-have #2, an extra column after the brief's).

+- Rates follow the probe: TPM binds at ~4 answers/minute, so steady = 3/min, overload = 12/min. Burst = steady plus 20 at once at 1:00. "Halved" halves the stand-in's RPM/TPM *without telling our limiter*, which must learn from headers and 429s. "Daily-exhausted" starts the stand-in's RPD at 0 with the 86.4 s trickle.

+- The naive-retry run is any scenario with `-policy naive`, so the comparison holds arrivals, seed and provider fixed. The naive policy also skips the limiter-wide pause on a 429 (otherwise our limiter would quietly make it polite).
+- Eval runs the questions closed loop, one at a time, so Table 3 latencies are the pipeline's, not a queue's. Grading: every key phrase present and a citation from the expected paper.
+- Only `eval` and `steady` may run against real Groq; the rest are refused on `-source real` to protect the shared daily budget.
+- First token for timeouts/errors is empty: the person saw no answer.
+**Cost:** Patience is a fixed 20 s for everyone (a guess, DESIGN §5); the runs show what it costs. Stand-in answer grades are meaningless (D9).

content.text:
The load generator is built and committed (`914284b`), and `make check` passes.

## What each piece does
**[internal/loadgen/schedule.go](internal/loadgen/schedule.go)**
- `Arrivals` turns phases like "3 per minute for 5 minutes" into start times. Gaps between requests are random (a Poisson process), because real traffic clumps even at a steady average, and evenly spaced arrivals would flatter the system. The same seed gives the same schedule every time.
- `Burst` makes N requests at the same instant: "something broke, everyone asks at once".

**[internal/loadgen/run.go](internal/loadgen/run.go)**
- `Execute` is the open loop. It starts each request at its scheduled time in its own goroutine, never waiting for earlier ones. Latency runs from the **scheduled** time, so if we're slow, it counts against us.
- `row` maps a reply to a CSV row. If the person saw no answer (timeout or error), `first_token_ms` is left empty.

**[internal/eval/grade.go](internal/eval/grade.go)**
- `Grade` marks an answer correct only if every key phrase is present **and** it cites a chunk from the right paper. Refusals are scored `refused_correctly` or `refused_wrongly`, and any answer to an unanswerable question is `wrong`.

**[cmd/loadgen](cmd/loadgen/main.go)**
- Runs one scenario and appends its rows to `results/results.csv`.
- The stand-in runs in-process on a free port.
- Only `eval` and `steady` may use real Groq, which protects the shared daily budget.

**The scenarios**, set by the probe's figure of about 4 answers a minute:
| Scenario | Shape |
|---|---|
| steady | 3/min for 5 min |
| burst | 3/min, plus 20 at once at 1:00 |
| overload | 12/min (3× capacity), 2% 5xx, 1% dropped connections |
| halved | the provider halves its limits **without telling our limiter** |
| daily-exhausted | the provider has no requests left today; one trickles back every 86.4s |
| `-policy naive` | works on any scenario, for the "retrying made it worse" comparison |

**Fixed along the way:** the naive policy needed one more change in the pipeline. Without it, our limiter-wide pause on a 429 would have quietly made the naive run polite, and the comparison would have shown nothing.

## Smoke run on the calibrated stand-in
8 requests, never more than 1ms late:
- 5 were served at once, in about 0.5s each.
- 2 were refused at the threshold with no tokens spent.
- Request 7 waited 3.2s because TPM was nearly used up.
- Request 8 was stepped down to **L1**, queued 14.8s, and finished in 15.3s, within its 20s patience.

## Order for Phase 9
1. **Your questions** replace the placeholders. Graded runs with mine can't go in the tables.
2. **Real eval on the dev half** × R1/R2/R3: tune threshold T and choose a setting. About 30 to 60 real calls.
3. **Held-out eval** with the chosen T, for the reported numbers.
4. **Stand-in scenarios** with the final T and setting, about 25 minutes in total. These can run in the background.
5. **One small real steady run.**

The order matters because T decides how many questions reach the model at all. Running the load scenarios before T is tuned would mean running them again.

"""Print the brief's results tables from results.csv, and nothing else.

Usage: python3 scripts/tables.py [results/results.csv]

Every number here is computed from that one file, so a reviewer can
recompute it. Percentiles are nearest-rank. Times in ms, percentages to
one decimal. "not measured" where a cell has no rows behind it.
"""

import csv
import math
import sys
from collections import defaultdict

NM = "not measured"


def pct(values, p):
    """Nearest-rank percentile: the smallest value with at least p% of
    values at or below it. None for an empty list."""
    if not values:
        return None
    s = sorted(values)
    rank = max(1, math.ceil(p / 100 * len(s)))
    return s[rank - 1]


def ms(v):
    return NM if v is None else str(int(v))


def triple(values, ps=(50, 95, 99)):
    if not values:
        return NM
    return " / ".join(ms(pct(values, p)) for p in ps)


def share(n, total):
    return NM if total == 0 else f"{100 * n / total:.1f}"


def num(row, col):
    v = row.get(col, "")
    return None if v == "" else float(v)


def load(path):
    with open(path, newline="") as f:
        return list(csv.DictReader(f))


def by(rows, key):
    groups = defaultdict(list)
    for r in rows:
        groups[key(r)].append(r)
    return dict(sorted(groups.items()))


def duration_s(rows):
    """Span of scheduled starts: how long the load was offered."""
    from datetime import datetime
    ts = [datetime.fromisoformat(r["start_time"].replace("Z", "+00:00")) for r in rows]
    return (max(ts) - min(ts)).total_seconds()


def table_2a(rows):
    out = ["| Scenario | Real or stand-in | Requests sent | Duration (s) | Offered rate (per min) | First token p50 / p95 / p99 (ms) | Total time p50 / p95 / p99 (ms) |",
           "|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|"]
    for (scen, src), rs in by(rows, lambda r: (r["scenario"], r["source"])).items():
        d = duration_s(rs)
        rate = NM if d == 0 else f"{60 * len(rs) / d:.1f}"
        first = [num(r, "first_token_ms") for r in rs if num(r, "first_token_ms") is not None]
        total = [num(r, "total_ms") for r in rs]
        out.append(f"| {scen} | {src} | {len(rs)} | {d:.0f} | {rate} | {triple(first)} | {triple(total)} |")
    return out


def answered(r):
    """A model answer was produced and shown (not a refusal, L2 or L3)."""
    return r["status"] == "ok" and int(num(r, "tokens_out") or 0) > 0


def table_2b(rows):
    out = ["| Scenario | Succeeded % | Rate-limited % | Timed out or given up % | Retries per request | Peak queue length | Tokens per answer | Cost per 1,000 answers |",
           "|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|"]
    for (scen, src), rs in by(rows, lambda r: (r["scenario"], r["source"])).items():
        n = len(rs)
        status = defaultdict(int)
        for r in rs:

        retries = sum(num(r, "retries") or 0 for r in rs) / n

"""Choose the refusal threshold T from a T=0 eval run on the dev half.

Usage: python3 scripts/tune_t.py results/results.csv eval/questions.json

With T=0 every question reached the model, and each row recorded its
top_norm. A threshold T would have refused, without a model call, every
question whose top_norm < T. This replays that for a grid of T values:
no extra calls are needed to compare thresholds.
"""

import csv
import json
import sys
from collections import defaultdict


def replay(rows, t):
    """Grades as they would be under threshold t."""
    out = []
    for r in rows:
        if float(r["top_norm"]) < t:
            out.append("refused_wrongly" if r["_answerable"] else "refused_correctly")
        else:
            out.append(r["answer_grade"])
    return out

import unittest

from tables import answered, pct, table_2b, table_3, triple


def row(**kw):
    base = {"request_id": "r", "scenario": "s", "source": "stand-in", "start_time": "2026-11-12T10:00:00Z",
            "first_token_ms": "100", "total_ms": "100", "status": "ok", "retries": "0", "tokens_in": "1000",
            "tokens_out": "100", "retrieval_setting": "R2", "answer_grade": "", "queue_len_at_arrival": "0",
            "queue_wait_ms": "0", "model_ms": "90"}
    base.update(kw)
    return base


class Percentile(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_nearest_rank(self):
        xs = [15, 20, 35, 40, 50]
        self.assertEqual(pct(xs, 50), 35)
        self.assertEqual(pct(xs, 95), 50)
        self.assertEqual(pct(xs, 1), 15)
        self.assertIsNone(pct([], 50))

    def test_triple_not_measured(self):
        self.assertEqual(triple([]), "not measured")


class Tables(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_2b_counts_and_tokens_only_over_answers(self):
        rows = [row(), row(status="rate_limited", tokens_in="0", tokens_out="0", queue_len_at_arrival="7"),
                row(status="timeout", retries="2", tokens_in="0", tokens_out="0"), row(tokens_out="0", tokens_in="0")]
        line = table_2b(rows)[2]
        # 3 of 4... no: statuses are ok, rate_limited, timeout, ok -> 50% ok.
        self.assertIn("| s (stand-in) | 50.0 | 25.0 | 25.0 | 0.50 | 7 | 1100 |", line)

    def test_answered_excludes_refusals(self):
        self.assertTrue(answered(row()))
        self.assertFalse(answered(row(tokens_out="0")))
        self.assertFalse(answered(row(status="rate_limited")))

    def test_3_grades(self):
        rows = [row(answer_grade="correct"), row(answer_grade="wrong"),
                row(answer_grade="refused_correctly", tokens_out="0"), row(answer_grade="refused_wrongly", tokens_out="0")]
        self.assertIn("| R2 | 4 | 25.0 | 25.0 | 25.0 | 1100 |", table_3(rows)[2])


if __name__ == "__main__":

cat > results/eval_review.md <<'EOF'
# Manual review of graded eval rows

DESIGN §7: a script grades (all key phrases present + a citation from the expected paper); I read every row where it might be wrong. **Grades in `results.csv` are left as the script gave them** so the tables stay recomputable; disagreements are recorded here.

**These rows use the 20 PLACEHOLDER questions** (`author: placeholder` in `eval/questions.json`), not the final hand-written set.

## Dev run, T = 0, 2026-11-12

The dev run (`eval-R1/R2/R3-*`) predates the answers log, so its answer texts were not saved. The three R2 rows below were re-asked with `cmd/relay -setting R2 -t 0` (temperature 0) and read; the answers may differ slightly from the graded run.

| Question | Script grade (R2) | My reading | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| q02 big Transformer parameters (213) | refused_wrongly | **agree** | The number is only in Table 3, flattened by pdftotext into number soup. The model refused instead of guessing: a safe failure. Table-only facts are a retrieval/parsing limit. |
| q04 Moshi Inner Monologue | wrong | **disagree: correct** | Answer names the Inner Monologue and the text stream generated as the first subsequence, both cited correctly. It says "text stream" where the key phrase says "text tokens": the key phrase was too narrow. |
| q05 H-Net chunk boundaries | wrong | **partly correct** | Says a boundary is set when similarity drops and the probability passes 0.5, cited to §2.2.1, but never names cosine similarity between adjacent vectors. Incomplete, not false. |

**Lesson for the final questions:** key phrases must be words any correct answer must use, not the paper's exact term for a concept a correct answer could name differently.

Also seen: the q05 re-ask hit a real Groq 429. Each `cmd/relay` run starts a fresh limiter that knows nothing of the previous processes' tokens that minute; Groq refused, and the retry honoured the 2 s hint and succeeded.
EOF
cat >> DECISIONS.md <<'EOF'

## D15 — 2026-11-12 — Setting R1, threshold T = 0.13 (from the dev half, placeholder questions)

**Measured** (real Groq, dev half, T = 0, `results.csv` rows `eval-R*`): R1 and R2 both 4 correct / 2 wrong / 3 correctly refused of 10; R3 2 / 3 / 3. Tokens per answer R1 1,999, R2 2,438, R3 1,785. Model time p50 R1 730 ms, R2 1,333 ms.
**Decision:** R1 (≈150-word pieces, 6 fetched). Same quality as R2 on dev with 18% fewer tokens, and tokens per minute is the limit that binds (D6), so R1 serves more answers per minute.
**T = 0.13:** between the off-topic question's top score (0.10–0.12) and the lowest answerable dev question (0.154). The model itself refused all three unanswerable dev questions, so T is a token saver for clearly off-topic questions, not the safety net; verify and the model's own refusal are. Raising T to 0.30 would have removed R2's two wrong answers on dev but refused three answerable ones, and is fitted to two questions.
**Cost:** Ten dev questions decide this; the margin between R1 and R2 is noise-sized. Two of the "wrong" grades are grader strictness (see `results/eval_review.md`). Closed-loop eval latency is dominated by waiting for TPM refill (slowest dev answer: 31.2 s queue, 1.5 s model).
**Caveat:** decided on placeholder questions; redo with the final set.
EOF

lines: - First token for timeouts/errors is empty: the person saw no answer.
**Cost:** Patience is a fixed 20 s for everyone (a guess, DESIGN §5); the runs show what it costs. Stand-in answer grades are meaningless (D9).
+## D15 — 2026-11-12 — Setting R1, threshold T = 0.13 (from the dev half, placeholder questions)

+**Measured** (real Groq, dev half, T = 0, `results.csv` rows `eval-R*`): R1 and R2 both 4 correct / 2 wrong / 3 correctly refused of 10; R3 2 / 3 / 3. Tokens per answer R1 1,999, R2 2,438, R3 1,785. Model time p50 R1 730 ms, R2 1,333 ms.
+**Decision:** R1 (≈150-word pieces, 6 fetched). Same quality as R2 on dev with 18% fewer tokens, and tokens per minute is the limit that binds (D6), so R1 serves more answers per minute.

+**T = 0.13:** between the off-topic question's top score (0.10–0.12) and the lowest answerable dev question (0.154). The model itself refused all three unanswerable dev questions, so T is a token saver for clearly off-topic questions, not the safety net; verify and the model's own refusal are. Raising T to 0.30 would have removed R2's two wrong answers on dev but refused three answerable ones, and is fitted to two questions.

+**Cost:** Ten dev questions decide this; the margin between R1 and R2 is noise-sized. Two of the "wrong" grades are grader strictness (see `results/eval_review.md`). Closed-loop eval latency is dominated by waiting for TPM refill (slowest dev answer: 31.2 s queue, 1.5 s model).
+**Caveat:** decided on placeholder questions; redo with the final set.
+# Manual review of graded eval rows

+DESIGN §7: a script grades (all key phrases present + a citation from the expected paper); I read every row where it might be wrong. **Grades in `results.csv` are left as the script gave them** so the tables stay recomputable; disagreements are recorded here.
+**These rows use the 20 PLACEHOLDER questions** (`author: placeholder` in `eval/questions.json`), not the final hand-written set.

+The dev run (`eval-R1/R2/R3-*`) predates the answers log, so its answer texts were not saved. The three R2 rows below were re-asked with `cmd/relay -setting R2 -t 0` (temperature 0) and read; the answers may differ slightly from the graded run.
+| Question | Script grade (R2) | My reading | Why |

+| q02 big Transformer parameters (213) | refused_wrongly | **agree** | The number is only in Table 3, flattened by pdftotext into number soup. The model refused instead of guessing: a safe failure. Table-only facts are a retrieval/parsing limit. |

+| q04 Moshi Inner Monologue | wrong | **disagree: correct** | Answer names the Inner Monologue and the text stream generated as the first subsequence, both cited correctly. It says "text stream" where the key phrase says "text tokens": the key phrase was too narrow. |

+| q05 H-Net chunk boundaries | wrong | **partly correct** | Says a boundary is set when similarity drops and the probability passes 0.5, cited to §2.2.1, but never names cosine similarity between adjacent vectors. Incomplete, not false. |
+**Lesson for the final questions:** key phrases must be words any correct answer must use, not the paper's exact term for a concept a correct answer could name differently.

+Also seen: the q05 re-ask hit a real Groq 429. Each `cmd/relay` run starts a fresh limiter that knows nothing of the previous processes' tokens that minute; Groq refused, and the retry honoured the 2 s hint and succeeded.

input.content:
# The Relay

A Go pipeline that answers questions about three arXiv papers with verified citations, a traffic controller that keeps it inside Groq's free-tier limits, and a small lab to test it: a stand-in model server, an open-loop load generator, and a recorder that writes `results/results.csv`.

One rule drives every choice: **under pressure the Relay gives less, never something wrong.**

Design: [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md). Every change since, with its cost: [DECISIONS.md](DECISIONS.md). Probe findings and Table 1: [results/probe/README.md](results/probe/README.md).

## Requirements

- Go 1.27+, Python 3, `pdftotext` (poppler)
- `GROQ_API_KEY` in the environment, only for real runs. Tests never call Groq.

## Layout

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|

content.text:
All Phase 9 runs have finished and the raw results are committed (`3e69f4a`), but they exposed two bugs I haven't fixed yet.

## What has run
| Run | Source | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Dev eval × R1/R2/R3 (30) | real | R1 chosen, T = 0.13 (D15) |
| Held-out eval, R1 (10) | real | 3 correct, 1 wrong, 3 correctly refused, **3 wrongly refused** |
| Steady (16) | real | 13 ok, **1 timeout, 2 dropped connections**: real failures, though the probe's 61 calls saw none |
| Steady (15) | stand-in | 15/15 ok, p50 448ms |
| Burst (32) | stand-in | 17 L0, 1 L1, 14 L2 "busy", slowest 7.6s, 0 provider 429s |
| Overload (48), with and without the naive policy | stand-in | 25 L0, 9 L1, 13 L2, 1 timeout; **identical in both** |
| Halved (12), with and without the naive policy | stand-in | Naive: 3 429s and 2 retries vs 1 429s and 0 retries; slowest 11.8s vs 9.5s |

`results/results.csv` now has 223 rows. The answer texts are in `results/answers.jsonl`.

## Bug 1: verify rejected correct quotes because of one character
All 3 wrongly refused held-out answers were correct. The model wrote "Mamba‑2", "self‑supervised" and "H‑Net" with a **non-breaking hyphen** (U+2011), while the paper uses a plain hyphen. My typography normaliser handles three kinds of dash but not that one. The fix is one line plus a regression test, and it would likely turn 3 refusals into correct answers.
- One honest caveat: I found this by looking at **held-out** failures, so a rerun of held-out isn't fully clean. I'll record that.

## Bug 2: the daily-exhausted run gave "busy" instead of passages
When the stand-in's daily budget ran out, the 429 came with an 87s retry hint. The limiter reported the *pause* as the reason, because 87s is slightly longer than the 86.4s daily refill. So two people got L2 ("try again in 44s") instead of L3 (cited passages), which is the rung designed for this case.
- The fix: when a daily limit is blocking, report the day as the reason, not the pause.
- I kept that run separately in `results/buggy/` as evidence, not in `results.csv`.

## What the naive-retry comparison actually shows
- **Overload is identical with and without the naive policy.** Our limiter stops calls before the provider can refuse them, so the retry policy barely matters there.
- **The harm only shows in "halved"**, where the provider changes its limits without telling us. One request with the naive policy retried after a fixed 1s into a still-full bucket, got refused twice more, and ended later than the polite version. That's a real but small case of retrying making things worse, and I'll present it as small.

## Budget
About **160K of roughly 200K daily tokens** are used: 134K recorded, plus about 25K from manual checks. The 200K TPD figure comes from Groq's docs and isn't measured.
- Rerunning just the held-out half would cost about 25K, so it fits, but only just.
- The daily-exhausted rerun is stand-in only and costs nothing.

content.text:
Fixing both bugs, each with a regression test, then rerunning only the affected runs. One bookkeeping decision first, so the tables stay honest:

- **The pre-fix held-out rows get moved** to `results/buggy/` as superseded, the same way as the daily-exhausted run. No values are changed. A held-out run done with a known verify bug shouldn't be mixed into Table 3.

cat >> DECISIONS.md <<'EOF'

## D16 — 2026-11-12 — Fixes found by the Phase 9 runs, and what was re-run

**Bugs the runs exposed (each fixed with a regression test that fails on the old code):**
1. *Verify refused correct quotes over one character.* The model writes U+2011 (non-breaking hyphen) in "Mamba‑2", "self‑supervised", "H‑Net"; the papers use plain hyphens. All three `refused_wrongly` rows of the first held-out run were correct answers. Every Unicode hyphen and dash now normalises to "-".
2. *A 429 pause hid the daily limit.* In the daily-exhausted run Groq-shaped 87 s retry hints outlasted the 86.4 s day refill, the limiter named the pause as the reason, and two people got L2 "busy" instead of L3 passages. A blocking day limit is now always the reason.
3. *Request ids were not unique.* The eval loop starts one run per question and ids restarted at 0000; two questions in the same second shared an id. Ids now use a process-wide counter.

**Data handling (no measured value changed):** the first held-out run and the buggy daily-exhausted run are moved to `results/buggy/` as superseded. Eval rows are now labelled by split (`eval-dev`, `eval-heldout`); the 30 existing dev rows were relabelled from `eval` (they came from `-split dev`). The one duplicate id got a `-b` suffix.
**Re-run:** held-out (real) and daily-exhausted (stand-in). **Not re-run:** the real steady run (budget: ~160K of ~200K daily tokens used); two of its answers (q06, q14) were refused by bug 1, and it is not graded.
**Caveat:** bug 1 was found by reading held-out failures, so the re-run held-out half is no longer fully untouched by tuning. The fix is general (Unicode normalisation), not fitted to those questions.
EOF
make check 2>&1 | grep -E 'FAIL|gofmt needed'; git add -A DECISIONS.md results internal/loadgen cmd/loadgen && git commit -q -m "Unique request ids; label eval rows by split; set aside superseded runs

The first held-out run (verify hyphen bug) and the daily-exhausted run
(L2 instead of L3) move to results/buggy/. Dev rows relabelled
eval-dev; one duplicate id suffixed. Values unchanged. See D16." && git log --oneline | head -1

Both fixes are in, each with a regression test that I checked fails on the old code and passes on the new: verify now handles every kind of Unicode hyphen, and a blocking daily limit is reported as the reason even when a 429 pause is longer. While doing that I found and fixed a third bug: request IDs could repeat.

**Reruns:** the real held-out eval and the stand-in daily-exhausted scenario are running now. They take about 3–6 minutes, and I'll merge them and print the tables when they finish.

**Data cleanup, with no measured values changed** (recorded in D16):
- The first held-out run and the buggy daily-exhausted run are moved to `results/buggy/` as superseded.
- The 30 dev rows are relabelled `eval-dev`, so tuning rows and reported rows can't mix in Table 3.
- The one duplicate request ID has a `-b` suffix.

My first attempt at the relabel wrote Windows line endings and changed every line of the file. I caught it in the diff, restored the file, and redid it.

**One caveat for the write-up:** I found the hyphen bug by reading held-out failures, so the held-out rerun isn't fully untouched by tuning. The fix itself is general, not fitted to those questions.

lines: **Bugs the runs exposed (each fixed with a regression test that fails on the old code):**

1. *Verify refused correct quotes over one character.* The model writes U+2011 (non-breaking hyphen) in "Mamba‑2", "self‑supervised", "H‑Net"; the papers use plain hyphens. All three `refused_wrongly` rows of the first held-out run were correct answers. Every Unicode hyphen and dash now normalises to "-".

2. *A 429 pause hid the daily limit.* In the daily-exhausted run Groq-shaped 87 s retry hints outlasted the 86.4 s day refill, the limiter named the pause as the reason, and two people got L2 "busy" instead of L3 passages. A blocking day limit is now always the reason.
-3. *Request ids were not unique.* The eval loop starts one run per question and ids restarted at 0000; two questions in the same second shared an id. Ids now use a process-wide counter.

+3. *A refund undid the provider's correction.* Re-running daily-exhausted after fix 2 still gave L2: on a 429 the pipeline applied the headers ("0 requests left today") and then refunded the refused call, adding one back. Settling now refunds first and applies headers last, since headers describe the state after the call. Fix 2 was real but was not what caused this symptom; a test reproducing the run found it.
+4. *Request ids were not unique.* The eval loop starts one run per question and ids restarted at 0000; two questions in the same second shared an id. Ids now use a process-wide counter.

**Data handling (no measured value changed):** the first held-out run and the buggy daily-exhausted run are moved to `results/buggy/` as superseded. content.text:
Both bugs are fixed and both affected runs reran; the latest commit is `1d43ead`. The reruns turned up two more bugs, also fixed with regression tests, and every table now prints from `results.csv`.

## The four fixes
Each has a regression test that I checked fails on the old code and passes on the new.

1. **Verify rejected non-breaking hyphens.** The model writes U+2011 in "Mamba‑2"; the papers use a plain hyphen. Held-out q14, q16 and q17 are no longer refused.
2. **A long 429 pause hid the daily limit.** A blocking daily limit is now always reported as the reason.
3. **A refund undid Groq's correction. This was the real cause of the daily-exhausted problem**, and fix 2 alone didn't solve it. On a 429, the code applied the headers ("0 requests left today") and then refunded the refused call, adding one back. Headers now go last. I found it by reproducing the run in a test instead of guessing a second time.
4. **The grader had the same hyphen bug as verify.** Verify and grading now share one normalisation package, `internal/textnorm`.

## Daily-exhausted now behaves as designed
After the first 429, every request gets **L3: cited passages, zero tokens**. One request was served from the single request that refills every 86.4s.

## Held-out, read by hand
| | Script | My reading |
|---|---|---|
| Correct | 4 | 6 |
| Partly correct | | 1 (q15) |
| Wrong | 4 | **1 (q19)** |
| Correctly refused | 2 | 2 |

**q19 is the most useful row in the whole set.** It's an unanswerable question about H-Net's latency in spoken dialogue. The words "real-time spoken dialogue" pulled in Moshi chunks, and the model answered "160ms", citing Moshi. The quote is real, so verify passed it. That's the documented limit, *true quote, false claim*, actually happening. A cheap fix would be to refuse when the question names one paper and the answer cites another; I wrote it down but didn't build it.

## Findings for the write-up
- **The limiter prevents provider 429s,** so `overload` and `overload-naive` came out identical. The naive policy only does damage when the provider changes its limits without notice (`halved`): 3 429s vs 1, and a slowest request of 11.8s vs 9.5s. That's a real but small effect.
- **In the real steady run, waiting dominates latency:** p50 2.2s, p95 12.3s, nearly all of it queueing for per-minute token refills. That run also saw 1 timeout and 2 dropped connections from Groq, failures the probe's 61 calls never saw.

**Budget:** about 185K of roughly 200K daily tokens are used, so there are no more real runs today. Real runs with your own questions need tomorrow's budget.

# The Relay — write-up

> **DRAFT.** Sections marked **[YOU: …]** need your own words. Graded results use the 20 **placeholder** questions (`author: placeholder`); replace them and re-run `eval` before submitting. Every number here is recomputable with `python3 scripts/tables.py results/results.csv`.

## 1. What I built and why

A Go pipeline over the three papers: **rewrite** (rules) → **retrieve** (own BM25, the tool call) → **decide** (refuse with no model call if the best normalised score < T) → **draft** (one Groq call, `gpt-oss-20b`) → **verify** (string checks, at most one redraft). In front of the model sits a traffic controller: token-bucket **limiter**, **retry** policy, one FIFO **admission** queue and a four-rung **ladder** (L0 full, L1 fewer chunks/no redraft, L2 "busy, try in N s", L3 cited passages with no model call).

**The decision that shaped it most: under pressure the Relay gives less, never something wrong.** Answers are buffered until verified: every sentence must carry a chunk id, cited ids must have been retrieved, every quote must appear in its chunk word for word (after typography normalisation), and at least one 3+ word quote must back the answer. Uncited sentences are deleted, not shown. I gave up time-to-first-token for this: the person's first token *is* the whole verified answer.

## 2. The real service and my stand-in

I measured limits with 61 planned calls (`cmd/probe`, raw in `results/probe/`), not from memory:

| Limit | Value found | How I found it | Confidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Requests per minute | 30 | 429 body "RPM: Limit 30, Used 30"; docs agree. A burst of 35 got 34 through | Value high; enforcement low |
| Tokens per minute | 8,000 | `x-ratelimit-limit-tokens`; 8 concurrent 1.28K-token calls: 6 ok, 2 refused, as predicted | High |
| Requests per day | 1,000 | `x-ratelimit-limit-requests`; `reset-requests` grows 86.4 s per call: refills one per 86.4 s | High |
| Tokens per day | 200,000 | Docs only; no header | Low: not measured |
| Requests in flight at once | No cap seen up to 35 | 35 concurrent calls | Low |
| What it returns when a limit is hit | HTTP 429, `retry-after` in whole seconds, JSON naming the limit and a precise wait; in 62–237 ms | Captured bodies | High |
| Time until it recovers | RPM 2 s; TPM = shortfall ÷ 133 tokens/s (7.03 s for a 1,279-token call) | Poll after 429; 429-body arithmetic | Medium |

**Stand-in** (`internal/standin`, same wire format, so the client cannot tell): first-token delay resampled from the probe, +0.05 ms per prompt token, +24 ms per other request in flight (a line through two bursts), 0.8 ms per output token; token-bucket limits with Groq-shaped headers and 429 bodies; 20 hidden reasoning tokens, so a tiny `max_tokens` returns an empty 200 exactly as Groq did; injectable 5xx and dropped connections. **Least like the real thing:** real slowness comes from other tenants, not my load; my limits are exact where Groq leaked 34 of 35; failure rates are chosen (the probe saw none, yet the real steady run then saw 1 timeout and 2 dropped connections in 16).

## 3. Results

Real = Groq free tier; stand-in = calibrated fake. "First token" is when the verified reply is released.

**Table 2a: Latency per load scenario**

| Scenario | Real or stand-in | Requests sent | Duration (s) | Offered rate (per min) | First token p50 / p95 / p99 (ms) | Total time p50 / p95 / p99 (ms) |

| Steady | real | 16 | 268 | 3.6 | 2171 / 12274 / 12274 | 2171 / 12274 / 12274 |

| Scenario | Succeeded % | Rate-limited % | Timed out or given up % | Retries per request | Peak queue length | Tokens per answer | Cost per 1,000 answers |

| Steady (real) | 81.2 | 0.0 | 6.2 | 0.44 | 0 | 2466 | $0.218 |
| Steady (stand-in) | 100.0 | 0.0 | 0.0 | 0.00 | 0 | 1416 | $0.116 |

| Daily budget exhausted | 28.6 | 71.4 | 0.0 | 0.00 | 0 | 1380 | $0.114 |

Real steady's missing 12.5% are 2 dropped connections (`error`). "Rate-limited" includes L2 and L3 replies: useful, but not model answers. **Answer quality** (held-out, 10 placeholder questions, script grades): 40% correct and cited, 40% wrong, 20% correctly refused, 2,012 tokens per answer. Reading every "wrong" row by hand (`results/eval_review.md`): 6 correct, 1 partly, **1 wrong**, 2 correctly refused; two "wrongs" were grader misses. **Numbers I could not have guessed:** Groq let 34 of 35 simultaneous calls through a 30 RPM limit; the day limit refills one request every 86.4 s rather than resetting; and three correct answers were refused over one character, U+2011, which the model writes in "Mamba‑2".

## 4. Where the time goes

Real steady, request `steady-R1-071824-0005`: 12,274 ms total = **11,868 ms waiting** in our queue for TPM to refill + **400 ms working** in the model + 6 ms ours, no retries. All the delay came **before the first token**: TPM (≈4 answers a minute) was spent by the requests ahead. I know from the per-row `queue_wait_ms` and `model_ms`, which the pipeline measures around `Acquire` and `Complete`. Retrying shows up in `halved-naive-…-0011`: 9,392 waiting + 397 working + **2,010 in two backoffs**.

## 5. When a limit is hit

**Per minute:** our limiter, not Groq, holds requests back (Groq's own RPM check leaked). On arrival, admission estimates the wait for this request *plus everyone queued ahead* and picks the best rung that still finishes inside the person's 20 s patience: wait for L0; take L1 (2 chunks, no redraft) if only that fits; otherwise L2 now, with N from the limiter (which includes Groq's retry hint). In the burst: 17 got L0, 1 L1, 14 an immediate L2, nobody timed out in the queue, 0 provider 429s. Who is dropped: only someone whose deadline passes while queued, and they leave the queue at that moment. **Per day:** every new request gets L3; running ones finish. The limiter learns it from the first 429's headers.

## Retrieval: quality versus cost

| Setting (piece size, pieces fetched, re-rank) | Questions asked | Correct and cited % | Wrong % | Correctly refused % | Tokens per answer | First token p50 / p95 (ms) | Total time p50 / p95 (ms) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| R1: ~150 words, 6, no (dev) | 10 | 40.0 | 20.0 | 30.0 | 1999 | 12243 / 21768 | 12243 / 21768 |
| R2: ~300 words, 4, no (dev) | 10 | 40.0 | 20.0 | 30.0 | 2438 | 16156 / 32763 | 16156 / 32763 |
| R3: ~300 words, 2, no (dev) | 10 | 20.0 | 30.0 | 30.0 | 1785 | 9311 / 24583 | 9311 / 24583 |
| R1 (held-out, chosen) | 10 | 40.0 | 40.0 | 20.0 | 2012 | 9095 / 25718 | 9095 / 25718 |

**I chose R1:** same quality as R2 on dev with 18% fewer tokens, and tokens per minute is the limit that binds, so R1 serves more people per minute. R3 is cheapest but two chunks often miss the answer. Latency here is mostly queueing for TPM even one question at a time (model time p50: R1 730 ms, R2 1,333 ms). **Near the limit**, L1 drops to 2 chunks and no redraft; at L3 retrieval *is* the answer. T = 0.13 was tuned on dev by replaying one T=0 run (`scripts/tune_t.py`): it saves tokens on clearly off-topic questions; it is not the safety net, because the model itself refused every unanswerable dev question.

## How this library will mislead a naive retriever

1. **Shared vocabulary across papers.** "What end-to-end latency does H-Net reach in real-time spoken dialogue?" — "real-time spoken dialogue" is Moshi's language, so BM25 fetched Moshi chunks and the model answered "160ms" citing Moshi. The quote was real, so verify passed it: our one genuinely wrong held-out answer.
2. **Facts that live only in tables.** "How many parameters does the big Transformer have?" — 213M appears only in Table 3, which `pdftotext` flattens into a run of numbers with no row labels; the model refused rather than guess.
3. **Page furniture.** Moshi prints its title on every page; left in, "What is Moshi?" matches every chunk equally. The parser drops lines repeated on over a third of pages.

## 6. Retries

Retry only 429, 5xx, timeouts and dropped connections, never other 4xx; at most 2; wait the provider's hint plus up to 500 ms jitter, else full-jitter exponential backoff (500 ms base, 8 s cap); never start a retry that cannot finish before the deadline. **Where retrying made it worse:** with Groq's limits silently halved, the naive policy (fixed 1 s, no jitter, hint ignored) retried into a still-empty bucket: request `…-0011` saw 3 429s instead of 1, spent 2,010 ms in backoff, and still failed, 11.8 s instead of 9.5 s. Honestly, the effect is small: under plain overload both policies gave identical results, because our limiter stopped calls from reaching Groq's 429s at all.

## 7. What the person sees

At 3 pm, daily budget gone, they get within ~20 ms, with zero tokens spent: *"Our daily model budget is used up, so I can't write an answer. These passages from the papers best match your question: 1. "…40 words…" [2410.00037v1, §3.3.1, p.10] …"* It only quotes the papers, so it cannot be wrong; it may simply not answer the question. One request trickles back every 86.4 s and is served normally.

## 8. What I'm unsure about, what I left out, what I learned

**Least certain assumption:** that people wait 20 s. If they give up at 5 s, almost every queued answer under load is lost, and the ladder must move to L1/L2 much earlier (admission takes patience as an input, so this is a number, not a redesign). **Deliberately not built:** embeddings or a re-ranker (BM25 plus verify was enough to stay correct; re-ranking would not fix q19), and a check that a cited chunk's paper matches a paper the question names (cheap, would have refused q19; found too late). **Also unsure:** whether Groq counts `max_tokens` at admission (evidence points both ways); slowdown-under-load is fitted to two points. **[YOU: one thing that was new to you, taught in your own words.]**

## Your feedback on Vaani

**[YOU: visit https://www.vaani.dev/ and write a few honest lines: what stood out, what confused you, one thing you would change.]**

## How I worked with the assistant

**[YOU: attach the real conversation history, then write this half page yourself.]** Facts you can draw on:
- *Prompts that mattered:* your design doc plus "under pressure give less, never wrong"; "run the probe" (turned assumptions into Table 1); "fix and rerun" after the first Phase 9 runs.
- *Things it got wrong that were caught:* verify let an uncited sentence through (caught on the first real Groq answer); a failed call's zero-value headers emptied the day budget (a test took 10 s instead of ms); its first fix for the L2-instead-of-L3 bug was not the real cause (a reproducing test found a refund undoing Groq's headers); it misread its own smoke-call data about `max_tokens` and corrected itself.
- *Where you overruled or directed:* you switched from writing the core files yourself to having them written and explained; you chose to run with placeholder questions.
- **[YOU: what in this submission is distinctly yours.]**

# The Relay — write-up

> **DRAFT.** **[YOU: …]** marks your own words. Graded rows use 20 **placeholder** questions; replace and re-run `eval` first. Every number: `python3 scripts/tables.py results/results.csv`. Reasons and costs of each choice: `DECISIONS.md`.

## 1. What I built and why

Go pipeline: **rewrite** (rules) → **retrieve** (own BM25, the tool call) → **decide** (refuse, no model call, if top normalised score < T) → **draft** (one Groq call) → **verify** (string checks, ≤1 redraft). In front: token-bucket **limiter**, **retry** policy, one FIFO **queue** and a ladder: L0 full, L1 fewer chunks/no redraft, L2 "busy, try in N s", L3 cited passages, no model call. **The deciding choice: under pressure give less, never something wrong.** Answers are held until verified (every sentence cited, cited chunks retrieved, quotes word for word in their chunk); uncited sentences are deleted. Cost: the first token *is* the whole answer.

## 2. The real service and my stand-in

| Limit | Value found | How found | Confidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Requests per minute | 30 | 429 body "RPM: Limit 30"; but 34 of a 35-call burst got through | Value high; enforcement low |
| Tokens per minute | 8,000 | header; 8 concurrent 1.28K-token calls: 6 ok, 2 refused, as predicted | High |
| Requests per day | 1,000 | header; reset grows 86.4 s per call: refills, no midnight reset | High |
| Tokens per day | 200,000 | docs only | Low: not measured |
| Requests in flight | no cap up to 35 | 35 concurrent calls | Low |
| When a limit is hit | 429 in 62–237 ms, `retry-after` (s), body names limit and exact wait | captured bodies | High |
| Time to recover | RPM 2 s; TPM shortfall ÷ 133 tok/s | poll; 429-body arithmetic | Medium |

61 planned calls (`cmd/probe`, raw in `results/probe/`). The **stand-in** speaks Groq's wire format: first-token delay resampled from the probe, +24 ms per other request in flight, Groq-shaped buckets, headers and 429s, hidden reasoning tokens (tiny `max_tokens` → empty 200, as on Groq), injectable failures. **Least like Groq:** real slowness comes from other tenants, not my load (my slowdown is a line through two bursts); its limits are exact where Groq leaked; failure rates are chosen, yet real steady then saw 3 failures in 16.

## 3. Results

| Scenario | Real or stand-in | Requests sent | Duration (s) | Offered rate (per min) | First token p50 / p95 / p99 (ms) | Total time p50 / p95 / p99 (ms) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Steady | real | 16 | 268 | 3.6 | 2171 / 12274 / 12274 | 2171 / 12274 / 12274 |
| Steady | stand-in | 15 | 277 | 3.3 | 448 / 688 / 688 | 448 / 688 / 688 |
| Burst (20 at once) | stand-in | 32 | 199 | 9.7 | 15 / 7479 / 7605 | 15 / 7479 / 7605 |
| Sustained overload | stand-in | 48 | 221 | 13.0 | 523 / 15175 / 19286 | 523 / 17585 / 20001 |
| Per-minute limit halved | stand-in | 12 | 199 | 3.6 | 450 / 9530 / 9530 | 450 / 9530 / 9530 |
| Halved, naive retries | stand-in | 12 | 199 | 3.6 | 448 / 11799 / 11799 | 448 / 11799 / 11799 |
| Daily budget exhausted | stand-in | 7 | 148 | 2.8 | 18 / 547 / 547 | 18 / 547 / 547 |

| Scenario | Succeeded % | Rate-limited % | Timed out or given up % | Retries per request | Peak queue length | Tokens per answer | Cost per 1,000 answers* |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Steady (real) | 81.2 | 0.0 | 6.2 | 0.44 | 0 | 2466 | $0.218 |
| Steady (stand-in) | 100.0 | 0.0 | 0.0 | 0.00 | 0 | 1416 | $0.116 |
| Burst | 56.2 | 43.8 | 0.0 | 0.00 | 2 | 1396 | $0.115 |
| Sustained overload | 70.8 | 27.1 | 2.1 | 0.04 | 3 | 1193 | $0.099 |
| Limit halved | 91.7 | 8.3 | 0.0 | 0.00 | 0 | 1424 | $0.117 |
| Halved, naive retries | 91.7 | 8.3 | 0.0 | 0.17 | 0 | 1424 | $0.117 |
| Daily budget exhausted | 28.6 | 71.4 | 0.0 | 0.00 | 0 | 1380 | $0.114 |

\*$0 on the free tier; shown at Groq's list price ($0.075/$0.30 per M in/out). First token = release of the verified reply; percentiles nearest-rank. Real steady's other 12.5% are dropped connections; "rate-limited" includes L2 and L3. **Quality**, held-out (10 questions, script): 40% correct and cited, 40% wrong, 20% correctly refused, 2,012 tokens/answer; read by hand, 6 correct, 1 partly, 1 wrong (`results/eval_review.md`). **Could not have guessed:** Groq's 30 RPM let 34 of 35 through; three correct answers were refused over one character, U+2011 in "Mamba‑2".

## 4. Where the time goes

Real steady `steady-R1-071824-0005`: 12,274 ms = **11,868 waiting** for TPM refill in our queue + **400 working** in the model + 6 ours, no retries: all before the first token. Measured per row around `Acquire` and `Complete` (`queue_wait_ms`, `model_ms`).

## 5. When a limit is hit

**Per minute:** our limiter holds requests (Groq's check leaked). Admission estimates the wait for a request *plus everyone queued ahead*, and gives the best rung that finishes within the person's 20 s: L0, else L1, else L2 at once with N from the limiter. Burst: 17 L0, 1 L1, 14 L2, none timed out, 0 provider 429s. Dropped: only someone whose deadline passes in the queue, who leaves it then. **Per day:** all new requests get L3; running ones finish.

## Retrieval: quality versus cost

| Setting (piece size, pieces, re-rank) | Questions asked | Correct and cited % | Wrong % | Correctly refused % | Tokens per answer | First token p50 / p95 (ms) | Total time p50 / p95 (ms) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| R1: 150 words, 6, no (dev) | 10 | 40.0 | 20.0 | 30.0 | 1999 | 12243 / 21768 | 12243 / 21768 |
| R2: 300 words, 4, no (dev) | 10 | 40.0 | 20.0 | 30.0 | 2438 | 16156 / 32763 | 16156 / 32763 |
| R3: 300 words, 2, no (dev) | 10 | 20.0 | 30.0 | 30.0 | 1785 | 9311 / 24583 | 9311 / 24583 |
| R1 (held-out, chosen) | 10 | 40.0 | 40.0 | 20.0 | 2012 | 9095 / 25718 | 9095 / 25718 |

**R1:** R2's quality with 18% fewer tokens, and tokens per minute is what binds. Latency is mostly TPM queueing (model p50 R1 730 ms, R2 1,333 ms). Near the limit L1 uses 2 chunks; at L3 retrieval is the answer. T = 0.13, tuned by replaying one T=0 dev run, only saves tokens: the model refused every unanswerable dev question itself.

## How this library will mislead a naive retriever

1. **Shared vocabulary.** "H-Net's latency in real-time spoken dialogue?" pulled Moshi chunks; the model answered "160ms" citing Moshi. Real quote, so verify passed it: our one wrong answer.
2. **Table-only facts.** "Parameters of the big Transformer?" — 213M lives in Table 3, flattened to unlabelled numbers; the model refused.
3. **Page furniture.** Moshi's title is on every page, so "What is Moshi?" matches every chunk; we strip repeated lines.

## 6. Retries

Only 429, 5xx, timeouts, dropped connections; ≤2; the provider's hint plus ≤500 ms jitter, else full-jitter backoff (500 ms–8 s); never if the deadline would pass. **Worse:** with limits silently halved, the naive policy (fixed 1 s, hint ignored) hit 3 429s instead of 1 on request `…-0011`, spent 2,010 ms backing off and still failed: 11.8 s vs 9.5 s. Small, honestly: under plain overload both policies tied, because our limiter kept calls away from Groq's 429s.

## 7. What the person sees

At 3 pm, in ~20 ms, zero tokens: *"Our daily model budget is used up, so I can't write an answer. These passages from the papers best match your question:"* then three cited excerpts. It quotes only the papers, so it cannot be wrong; it may not answer. One request returns every 86.4 s.

## 8. What I'm unsure about, what I left out, what I learned

**Least certain:** 20 s patience. At 5 s most queued answers under load are lost and the ladder must step down earlier (patience is an input, so a number, not a redesign). **Not built:** a re-ranker (would not fix q19) and a check that cited papers match the paper a question names (would have refused q19). **[YOU: one thing new to you, taught in your words.]**

## Your feedback on Vaani

**[YOU: a few honest lines after visiting vaani.dev: what stood out, what confused you, one change.]**

## How I worked with the assistant

**[YOU: attach the real history; write this in your words.]** Material: prompts that mattered (the design doc; "run the probe"; "fix and rerun"). Caught mistakes: verify passed an uncited sentence (first real answer); zero-value headers emptied the day budget (a 10 s test); a first L3 fix that wasn't the cause (a reproducing test found a refund undoing Groq's headers). Overruled/directed: you had the core files written and explained; you ran with placeholders.

# The Relay — write-up

> **DRAFT.** **[YOU: …]** marks your own words. Graded rows use 20 **placeholder** questions; replace and re-run `eval` first. Every number: `python3 scripts/tables.py results/results.csv`. Reasons and costs of each choice: `DECISIONS.md`.

## 1. What I built and why

Go pipeline: **rewrite** (rules) → **retrieve** (own BM25, the tool call) → **decide** (refuse, no model call, if top normalised score < T) → **draft** (one Groq call) → **verify** (string checks, ≤1 redraft). In front: token-bucket **limiter**, **retry** policy, one FIFO **queue** and a ladder: L0 full, L1 fewer chunks/no redraft, L2 "busy, try in N s", L3 cited passages, no model call. **The deciding choice: under pressure give less, never something wrong.** Answers are held until verified (every sentence cited, cited chunks retrieved, quotes word for word in their chunk); uncited sentences are deleted. Cost: the first token *is* the whole answer.

## 2. The real service and my stand-in

| Limit | Value found | How found | Confidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Requests per minute | 30 | 429 body "RPM: Limit 30"; but 34 of a 35-call burst got through | Value high; enforcement low |
| Tokens per minute | 8,000 | header; 8 concurrent 1.28K-token calls: 6 ok, 2 refused, as predicted | High |
| Requests per day | 1,000 | header; reset grows 86.4 s per call: refills, no midnight reset | High |
| Tokens per day | 200,000 | docs only | Low: not measured |
| Requests in flight | no cap up to 35 | 35 concurrent calls | Low |
| When a limit is hit | 429 in 62–237 ms, `retry-after` (s), body names limit and exact wait | captured bodies | High |
| Time to recover | RPM 2 s; TPM shortfall ÷ 133 tok/s | poll; 429-body arithmetic | Medium |

61 planned calls (`cmd/probe`, raw in `results/probe/`). The **stand-in** speaks Groq's wire format: first-token delay resampled from the probe, +24 ms per other request in flight, Groq-shaped buckets, headers and 429s, hidden reasoning tokens (tiny `max_tokens` → empty 200, as on Groq), injectable failures. **Least like Groq:** real slowness comes from other tenants, not my load (my slowdown is a line through two bursts); its limits are exact where Groq leaked; failure rates are chosen, yet real steady then saw 3 failures in 16.

## 3. Results

| Scenario | Real or stand-in | Requests sent | Duration (s) | Offered rate (per min) | First token p50 / p95 / p99 (ms) | Total time p50 / p95 / p99 (ms) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Steady | real | 16 | 268 | 3.6 | 2171 / 12274 / 12274 | 2171 / 12274 / 12274 |
| Steady | stand-in | 15 | 277 | 3.3 | 448 / 688 / 688 | 448 / 688 / 688 |
| Burst (20 at once) | stand-in | 32 | 199 | 9.7 | 15 / 7479 / 7605 | 15 / 7479 / 7605 |
| Sustained overload | stand-in | 48 | 221 | 13.0 | 523 / 15175 / 19286 | 523 / 17585 / 20001 |
| Per-minute limit halved | stand-in | 12 | 199 | 3.6 | 450 / 9530 / 9530 | 450 / 9530 / 9530 |
| Halved, naive retries | stand-in | 12 | 199 | 3.6 | 448 / 11799 / 11799 | 448 / 11799 / 11799 |
| Daily budget exhausted | stand-in | 7 | 148 | 2.8 | 18 / 547 / 547 | 18 / 547 / 547 |

| Scenario | Succeeded % | Rate-limited % | Timed out or given up % | Retries per request | Peak queue length | Tokens per answer | Cost per 1,000 answers* |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Steady (real) | 81.2 | 0.0 | 6.2 | 0.44 | 0 | 2466 | $0.218 |
| Steady (stand-in) | 100.0 | 0.0 | 0.0 | 0.00 | 0 | 1416 | $0.116 |
| Burst | 56.2 | 43.8 | 0.0 | 0.00 | 2 | 1396 | $0.115 |
| Sustained overload | 70.8 | 27.1 | 2.1 | 0.04 | 3 | 1193 | $0.099 |

\*$0 on the free tier; shown at Groq's list price ($0.075/$0.30 per M in/out). First token = release of the verified reply; percentiles nearest-rank. Real steady's other 12.5% are dropped connections; "rate-limited" includes L2 and L3. **Quality**, held-out (10 questions, script): 40% correct and cited, 40% wrong, 20% correctly refused, 2,012 tokens/answer; read by hand, 6 correct, 1 partly, 1 wrong (`results/eval_review.md`). **Could not have guessed:** Groq's 30 RPM let 34 of 35 through; three correct answers were refused over one character, U+2011 in "Mamba‑2".

## 4. Where the time goes

Real steady `steady-R1-071824-0005`: 12,274 ms = **11,868 waiting** for TPM refill in our queue + **400 working** in the model + 6 ours, no retries: all before the first token. Measured per row around `Acquire` and `Complete` (`queue_wait_ms`, `model_ms`).

## 5. When a limit is hit

**Per minute:** our limiter holds requests (Groq's check leaked). Admission estimates the wait for a request *plus everyone queued ahead*, and gives the best rung that finishes within the person's 20 s: L0, else L1, else L2 at once with N from the limiter. Burst: 17 L0, 1 L1, 14 L2, none timed out, 0 provider 429s. Dropped: only someone whose deadline passes in the queue, who leaves it then. **Per day:** all new requests get L3; running ones finish.

| R1 (held-out, chosen) | 10 | 40.0 | 40.0 | 20.0 | 2012 | 9095 / 25718 | 9095 / 25718 |

1. **Shared vocabulary.** "H-Net's latency in real-time spoken dialogue?" pulled Moshi chunks; the model answered "160ms" citing Moshi. Real quote, so verify passed it: our one wrong answer.
2. **Table-only facts.** "Parameters of the big Transformer?" — 213M lives in Table 3, flattened to unlabelled numbers; the model refused.
3. **Page furniture.** Moshi's title is on every page, so "What is Moshi?" matches every chunk; we strip repeated lines.

## 6. Retries

Only 429, 5xx, timeouts, dropped connections; ≤2; the provider's hint plus ≤500 ms jitter, else full-jitter backoff (500 ms–8 s); never if the deadline would pass. **Worse:** with limits silently halved, the naive policy (fixed 1 s, hint ignored) hit 3 429s instead of 1 on request `…-0011`, spent 2,010 ms backing off and still failed: 11.8 s vs 9.5 s. Small, honestly: under plain overload both policies tied, because our limiter kept calls away from Groq's 429s.

## 7. What the person sees

At 3 pm, in ~20 ms, zero tokens: *"Our daily model budget is used up, so I can't write an answer. These passages from the papers best match your question:"* then three cited excerpts. It quotes only the papers, so it cannot be wrong; it may not answer. One request returns every 86.4 s.

## 8. What I'm unsure about, what I left out, what I learned

**Least certain:** 20 s patience. At 5 s most queued answers under load are lost and the ladder must step down earlier (patience is an input, so a number, not a redesign). **Not built:** a re-ranker (would not fix q19) and a check that cited papers match the paper a question names (would have refused q19). **[YOU: one thing new to you, taught in your words.]**

These three sections are where reviewers look for *you*, so I'll give you angles and outlines rather than finished text. Each point is something that really happened in this project, so you can defend it live.

## §8: One thing that was new to you (2–3 lines)

Pick **one** of these, the one that genuinely surprised you, and explain it the way you would to a colleague.

**Option A: rate limits are buckets that refill, not counters that reset.**
- What you expected: "1,000 requests per day" resets at midnight.
- What the probe showed: `x-ratelimit-reset-requests` grew by 86.4s with every call, which is 86,400s ÷ 1,000. The allowance refills continuously.
- Why it matters: "daily budget exhausted" isn't a cliff. One request comes back every 86.4s, and both the limiter and the stand-in had to be built around that.

**Option B: "retry after 2 seconds" can cause the next overload.**
- If everyone who got a 429 retries after exactly 2 seconds, they all arrive together and cause the same pile-up again.
- The fix is jitter: wait the hint plus a small random extra, so retries spread out.
- Tie it to your measurement: the naive policy hit 3 429s where the jittered one hit 1.

**Option C: a slow load generator hides a slow system (open vs closed loop).**
- If the generator waits for each answer before sending the next, a slow system automatically gets less traffic, so it looks fine.
- Sending on a fixed schedule and timing from the *scheduled* start exposes queueing instead of hiding it.

A is the most yours, because it came from your own probe data. A rough skeleton:

When this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, it also holds one short question, the decision alone with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give, plus buttons of one to three words that answer it; a turn with nothing pending sends the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Your closing message follows the call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the box's recap never replaces. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR the app watches it and wakes you on CI failures, merge conflicts and review comments, so the box never offers to keep watching, poll or fix CI, in a question or a button. It asks only what the user must do or decide (an approval, a review request, a choice), as one question. Part of wrapping up is deciding, unasked, whether what the user asked for left a real follow-up, and where it runs; most turns leave none. One piece of work that acts on what this session just found stays here while this session has nothing else in flight ("Starting other sessions" says why): make it the box's question, with a button that has you do it here. tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

**Do not spawn agents unless the user asks.** Each spawn starts cold and re-derives context you already have — it's the expensive path on this plan. A task with "multiple angles," "thorough," or several parts is not a request to spawn; handle it inline with your own tools. Only use this tool when the user explicitly says to use a subagent, or names one of the available agent types. This does not cover the `web-fetch` agent type where it is listed and you have no WebFetch tool of your own: it stands in for that tool, so calling it to read a page is ordinary tool use.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

A fork runs in the background and keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate. Subagents run in the background; you'll be notified when one completes. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.
