tools.description: List network requests, or fetch a specific response body by `requestId`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__read_page
tools.description: Read the current page in the Browser pane as a YAML-style accessibility tree. Each interactive element is tagged `[ref_N]` for use with `computer`/`form_input`/`find`. Prefer this over screenshot for verifying text and structure. Output is limited to 50000 characters by default; if it exceeds the limit it is truncated with a note — pass a larger max_chars, or use ref_id/depth to focus.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

filter.description: 'interactive' returns only clickable/typable elements; 'all' (default) returns the full tree.

ref_id.description: Restrict the tree to descendants of this `ref_N` (from a previous read_page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

tools.description: Close one Browser pane tab. Closing the last tab closes the Browser pane itself (reopen it with `preview_start`).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__tabs_context
tools.description: List every Browser pane tab (origin only — titles are page-authored). Returns {browserOpen, tabs: [{tabId, origin, isActive}]} plus a line saying whether the pane is currently displayed or hidden (a hidden pane still works, but its page runs as a background page, so timing and performance numbers from it can be off; prefer `read_page` / `get_page_text` over screenshots while it is hidden). browserOpen is false (and tabs empty) until `preview_start` or `navigate` opens the pane, so you don't need to call this before opening it.

foreground.description: Front the new tab (user asked to see it or is following along). Default false: open behind the user's current tab.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control
tools.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'press_key' presses a hardware key 'count' times: return, delete (backspace), an arrow, select_all, undo or redo (a key also hides the on-screen keyboard); 'set_appearance' switches the device to light or dark mode; 'appearance' says which it is in; 'set_keyboard' shows or hides the on-screen keyboard (it appears only while a text field has focus, and 'press_key' and 'text' hide it again); 'rotate' turns the device a quarter turn left or right ('direction'); take a 'screenshot' after it and tap in that screenshot's frame, however it comes back; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). Start more than 4pt from the edge to drag or scroll content near the bezel.

app_path.description: For 'launch': absolute path (no ~) to the built .app bundle (e.g. /Users/me/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData/MyApp-abc123/Build/Products/Debug-iphonesimulator/MyApp.app).

device.description: Simulator name (e.g. 'iPhone 17 Pro') or UDID. Defaults to the simulator already attached, else the first booted one. The first use of a device asks the user for permission.

udid.description: Alias for 'device' (identical semantics: simulator name or UDID). Pass at most one of 'device' / 'udid'.

bundle_id.description: For 'launch': bundle identifier. If omitted, extracted from the .app's Info.plist.

points.description: For 'touch_path': touch path samples in device points. First point is touch-down; last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000 ms; the first sample's is skipped, so send 0 or omit it; at most 30 seconds in all).

points2.description: For 'touch2_path': two-finger path samples in device points. Each sample carries both contacts (x1/y1, x2/y2); first is touch-down, last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000 ms; the first sample's is skipped, so send 0 or omit it; at most 30 seconds in all).

duration.description: Seconds. For 'tap', >0.5 is a long-press. For 'swipe', the gesture duration (default 0.3).

key.description: For 'press_key': the key or edit command to press.

count.description: For 'press_key': how many times to press it, 1 to 20 (default 1).

state.description: For 'set_keyboard': 'show' or 'hide' the on-screen keyboard. For 'set_appearance': 'light' or 'dark'.

url.description: For 'open_url': URL or scheme to open in the simulator.

tools.description:
Show visual content — SVG graphics, diagrams, charts, or interactive HTML widgets — that renders inline alongside your text response.
Use for flowcharts, architecture diagrams, dashboards, forms, calculators, data tables, games, illustrations, or any visual content.
The code is auto-detected: starts with <svg = SVG mode, otherwise HTML mode.
A global sendPrompt(text) function is available — it sends a message to chat as if the user typed it.
IMPORTANT: Call read_me before your first show_widget call. Do NOT narrate or mention the read_me call to the user — call it silently, then respond as if you went straight to building the visualization.

loading_messages.description: 1–4 loading messages shown to the user while the visual renders, each roughly 5 words long. Write them in the same language the user is using. Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. Playful examples — revenue chart: ['Bribing bars to stand taller', 'Asking Q4 where it went']; kanban: ['Herding cards into columns', 'Dragging, dropping, not stopping'].

title.description: Short snake_case identifier for this visual. Must be specific and disambiguating — if the conversation has multiple visuals, this title alone should tell you which one is being referenced (e.g. 'q4_revenue_by_product_line' not 'chart', 'oauth_login_flow' not 'diagram'). Also used as the download filename, so no spaces or special characters.

widget_code.description: SVG or HTML code to render. For SVG: raw SVG code starting with <svg> tag, must use CSS variables for colors. Example: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">...</svg>. For HTML: raw HTML content to render, do NOT include DOCTYPE, <html>, <head>, or <body> tags. Use CSS variables for theming. Keep background transparent and avoid top-level padding. Scripts are supported but execute after streaming completes.

Result of calling the Read tool:
1	# The Relay: design (v1, simple, 6-hour build)
2	
3	Written 2026-11-12. Replaces the earlier long design. Anything marked **TBD** gets a number only after I measure something. Changes after today go into DECISIONS.md as new entries.
4	
5	## 1. What I'm building
6	
7	A Go pipeline that answers questions about three arXiv papers (1706.03762 v7, 2410.00037 v1, 2507.07955 v2), with a traffic controller for model rate limits, and a small lab to test it: a fake model server, a load generator and a recorder that writes `results.csv`.
8	
9	One rule drives every choice: **under pressure the Relay gives less, never something wrong.**
10	
11	Languages: **Go** for everything that runs. **Python** only for two jobs: parsing the PDFs into text with page and heading info, and turning `results.csv` into tables.
12	
13	## 2. Pipeline (5 steps, one model call)
14	
15	```
16	question
17	  1. Rewrite    question -> search query         (plain rules, no model)
18	  2. Retrieve   query -> top-k chunks            (TOOL CALL: own BM25, no model)
19	  3. Decide     best score < T ? refuse : go on  (BRANCH)
20	  4. Draft      chunks -> cited answer           (the one model call, streamed)
21	  5. Verify     check citations and quotes       (LOOP: at most 1 redraft)
22	  -> reply
23	```
24	
25	- **Rewrite by rules** (lowercase, drop filler words, keep technical terms). Cost I will state in the write-up: only one model call per answer, so the pipeline is less "chained" than the assistant in the brief. Gain: fewer tokens, fewer limit hits, simpler.
26	- **Decide:** if the best BM25 score is under threshold T, reply "the papers don't say". T is TBD, tuned on the dev half of the eval. Cost: some wrong refusals, counted as `refused_wrongly`.
27	- **Draft:** the model gets the chunks and must write short claims, each followed by a chunk id, with direct quotes in quotation marks.
28	- **Verify:** string checks, no model. Every cited id was retrieved. Every quote appears word for word (after whitespace normalisation) in the chunk it cites. At least one citation unless it is a refusal. If a check fails: redraft once naming the failure; if it fails again: reply "could not verify" (a refusal). Known limit: it can't catch a correct quote used for the wrong claim.
29	- **Release:** buffer the full answer, verify, then show it. So time to first token is close to total time. I accept this because it keeps the "never wrong" rule simple.
30	
31	## 3. Library and retrieval
32	
33	- **Python parse** (`scripts/parse.py`): `pdftotext` per paper at the pinned version, keep page breaks, detect numbered headings with a simple heuristic, write one JSON file per paper with pages and headings.
34	- **Go chunking:** cut pages into pieces of about N words with a small overlap, never inside a word. Each chunk has `chunk_id, paper, version, section, page_start, page_end, text`. Citation shown: `[1706.03762v7, §3.2.1, p.4]` (page only if no section found).
35	- **BM25** written by me, no embeddings, no vector DB. Tokenizer: lowercase, split on non-letters/digits, small stopword list.
36	- **Three retrieval settings** (starting guesses, may change after I see data), varying piece size and number of pieces only:
37	
38	| Setting | Piece size | Pieces fetched |
39	|---|---|---|
40	| R1 | about 150 words | 6 |
41	| R2 | about 300 words | 4 |
42	| R3 | about 300 words | 2 |
43	
44	No re-ranker. It is one of three allowed knobs and not worth the hours.
45	
46	## 4. Model client, probe and stand-in
47	
48	- **One `Client` interface**, two implementations over the same HTTP code: Groq and the stand-in (same request shape, same streaming, same rate-limit headers). The pipeline can't tell them apart. Both report: sent time, first piece time, finish time, token counts.
49	- **Errors are typed** (`RateLimitError{RetryAfter}`, `ServerError`, `TimeoutError`, `ClientError`) because retry depends on telling them apart.
50	- **Probe** (`cmd/probe`): a modest number of real calls on my own free account, some at higher concurrency. Save raw headers, timings and the exact 429 body to `results/probe/`. Read Groq's docs and write them next to what I saw. This fills Table 1 with a confidence label per row. No limit is written from memory.
51	- **Stand-in** (`cmd/standin`): a small HTTP server that
52	  - is **slow**: first-token and per-piece delays resampled from the probe data,
53	  - **slows under load**: extra delay grows with requests in flight (simple linear fit; marked low confidence if the probe can't support it),
54	  - **fails**: a set rate of 5xx and dropped connections,
55	  - **refuses at a limit**: per-minute requests, per-minute tokens, per-day requests, in-flight cap, with a 429 and headers shaped like the real one,
56	  - **streams** in pieces.
57	
58	  Config records which probe run each number came from. Write-up says where it is least like the real service (my guess to check: real slowness comes from other people's traffic; mine is a formula, and real limits can change).
59	
60	## 5. Traffic controller
61	
62	Kept small on purpose.
63	
64	- **Limiter:** sliding windows for requests per minute, tokens per minute, requests per day, plus a cap on in-flight. Before sending it reserves an estimate (input tokens + max output) and releases the difference when real usage arrives.
65	- **Good to have #1: header correction.** The limiter corrects its own count from the provider's rate-limit headers (names from the probe).
66	- **Queue and admission:** one bounded FIFO queue. On arrival, estimate the wait. If it is longer than the person's remaining patience, don't queue; take the next rung down the ladder. Expired requests are dropped from the queue immediately.
67	- **Deadlines** (TBD, my least certain assumption): first token and whole answer. Starting guesses to test against the probe.
68	- **A running request finishes** unless its deadline passes.
69	- **Degradation ladder** (4 levels; each gives less, none is wrong):
70	  - **L0** full pipeline
71	  - **L1** fewer chunks and no redraft (if verify fails, refuse)
72	  - **L2** "busy, try again in N seconds", N from the provider's retry hint, not a guess
73	  - **L3** daily budget gone: **no model call**. Return the top retrieved passages with citations and a plain note. Costs zero tokens and can't be wrong, since it only shows text from the papers. This is what the person sees when the budget is gone.
74	
75	  Skipping verify is not a rung: it saves nothing and risks a bad answer.
76	- **Per-minute limit hit:** the limiter holds requests back. Who waits, who gets L1, who gets L2 depends on remaining deadline. **Per-day limit hit:** every new request goes to L3; running ones finish if they can.
77	- **Retries:** only 429, 5xx, timeouts, dropped connections; never other 4xx. Honour the provider's retry hint, else exponential backoff with full jitter. At most 2 retries per call. Never retry if the deadline would pass first.
78	- **Naive-retry run** (required evidence that retrying can hurt): same overload scenario with fixed delay, no jitter, ignoring the retry hint. Compare it to the real policy.
79	
80	## 6. Load generator and results
81	
82	- **Open loop.** Requests start at scheduled times whether or not earlier ones finished. Latency is measured from the **scheduled** start, so a slow system can't hide itself.
83	- **Good to have #2: lag check.** Log how late each start was against the schedule, to show the generator wasn't the slow part.
84	- **Scenarios** (rates and durations TBD after the probe): steady (real small + stand-in larger), burst, sustained overload, per-minute limit halved, daily budget exhausted, plus the naive-retry overload run. That is five scenarios plus one, more than the three the brief asks for, but Table 2a lists them.
85	- **Real runs** share the daily allowance with the probe and eval. Plan the budget first: probe, then 3 settings x 20 questions, then one small steady run. If I hit the daily limit by accident, keep it as evidence.
86	- **`results.csv`**, one file, `source` column = real or stand-in. Required columns in this order:
87	  `request_id, scenario, source, start_time, first_token_ms, total_ms, status, retries, tokens_in, tokens_out, retrieval_setting, answer_grade`
88	  Extra columns after those (I'll say so in the write-up): `question_id, queue_wait_ms, model_ms, queue_len_at_arrival, ladder_level, n_429_seen, error_detail`
89	  - `status` is the final status: ok, rate_limited, timeout, error.
90	  - `answer_grade` only for eval rows: correct, wrong, refused_correctly, refused_wrongly.
91	- **Python `tables.py`** reads only `results.csv` and prints every table. I recompute two numbers by hand.
92	
93	## 7. Eval
94	
95	20 questions I write **before** looking at any retrieval output: 14 answerable (gold key phrases, expected paper and section), 6 not answerable (some close to the topic, to test T). Dev half to tune T and settings, held-out half to report. With 20 questions the numbers are rough, and I say so. Grading: a script checks key phrases and the cited chunk; I read every row where I disagree. Tokens per answer come from the provider's usage numbers.
96	
97	## 8. Good to haves (3, no more)
98	
99	1. Limiter corrected from provider headers (not guessed limits).
100	2. Open-loop generator with scheduled-start timing and lag check.
101	3. Retrieval-only last rung (L3): a useful reply at zero token budget.
102	
103	Stretch only if ahead: sentence-level release.
104	
105	## 9. Not building
106	
107	Embeddings, a model-based query rewriter, a re-ranker, a global retry budget, queue priorities, an agent framework, a dashboard, Docker, auto-tuning of limits.
108	
109	## 10. Hour budget: 6.0 (targets, not measured)
110	
111	| Work | Hours |
112	|---|---|
113	| Repo, `make check`, `.gitignore`, first DECISIONS entries | 0.3 |
114	| Groq account, docs, probe, Go streaming call, Table 1 | 0.6 |
115	| Python parse, Go chunking, chunk store | 0.4 |
116	| 20 eval questions with gold answers | 0.5 |
117	| BM25 + tests | 0.6 |
118	| Pipeline: decide, draft, verify + tests | 0.7 |
119	| Stand-in, calibrated | 0.5 |
120	| Limiter, queue/admission, retry, ladder + tests | 0.9 |
121	| Load generator + recorder | 0.4 |
122	| All runs (long ones in the background) | 0.3 |
123	| Tables script, write-up (2 pages), README, rehearsal | 0.8 |
124	| **Total** | **6.0** |
125	
126	If I fall behind, cut in this order: lag check, third retrieval setting, the "busy" rung. I don't cut tests, the 20 questions or any required table.
127	
128	## 11. Rules I keep
129	
130	- One free Groq account, mine. No tricks around limits. Key only in `GROQ_API_KEY`, never in a file, log or commit.
131	- Tests never call real Groq. They use the stand-in or fixed responses.
132	- Every table number is recomputable from `results.csv`. Anything unmeasured says "not measured".
133	- Before each commit: `gofmt -l .`, `go vet ./...`, `go test ./...`, and `-race` on limiter, queue, retry.
134	
135	## 12. Open items and how each gets settled
136	
137	| Item | Settled by |
138	|---|---|
139	| Streaming in Go works | first probe session; else a DECISIONS entry to switch |
140	| Header names, real limits, retry hint | probe, Table 1 |
141	| Deadlines | probe plus my judgement |
142	| Threshold T | dev half of the eval |
143	| Retrieval setting | Table 3 |
144	| Ladder triggers | which limit runs out first |
145	| Backoff base and cap | probe, overload run |
146	| Queue max length | burst and overload runs |
147

# Decisions

Changes to DESIGN.md after 2026-11-12 are recorded here, newest last. Each entry says what was decided, why, and what it costs.

## D1 — 2026-11-12 — Standard library only for Go

**Decision:** No third-party Go modules. HTTP, streaming (SSE line reading), CSV, JSON and tests all use the standard library.
**Why:** Every line that runs is code I can explain in the live session. BM25, the limiter and the retry policy are the point of the exercise; a library would hide them.
**Cost:** A little more code for SSE parsing and table-style tests.

## D2 — 2026-11-12 — `make check` is the commit gate

**Decision:** `make check` runs `gofmt -l`, `go vet`, `go test` and `go test -race` on every package. A versioned pre-commit hook (`.githooks/pre-commit`, enabled with `make hooks`) runs it.
**Why:** DESIGN.md §11 asks for these before every commit; a hook makes it impossible to forget.
**Cost:** `-race` on all packages instead of only limiter/queue/retry. Slower by seconds, which is fine at this size.

## D3 — 2026-11-12 — Layout

**Decision:** `cmd/` holds one binary per job (`relay`, `probe`, `standin`, `loadgen`). `internal/` holds the logic, one package per concern: `corpus`, `retrieve`, `llm`, `pipeline`, `traffic`, `results`. Python lives only in `scripts/`.
**Why:** Binaries stay thin; every package can be tested without a network.
**Cost:** None worth noting.

# The Relay

A Go pipeline that answers questions about three arXiv papers with citations, plus a traffic controller for model rate limits and a small lab (stand-in model server, open-loop load generator, recorder) to test it under load.

Design: [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md). Changes since: [DECISIONS.md](DECISIONS.md).

## Requirements

- Go 1.27+
- Python 3 and `pdftotext` (poppler) for parsing the papers
- A Groq API key in `GROQ_API_KEY` (only for real runs; tests never call Groq)

## Development

```bash
make hooks   # once: run `make check` before every commit
make check   # gofmt, go vet, go test, go test -race
```

# Probe results

Run `20261112T054119Z` (`calls.jsonl`): 61 real calls to `openai/gpt-oss-20b` on my free Groq account, `reasoning_effort: low`, from India (`x-groq-region: bom`). Plus one smoke call before it (not in the file). Docs read the same day: console.groq.com/docs/rate-limits.

## Table 1: Limits found in the real service

| Limit | Value found | How found | Confidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Requests per minute | 30 | 429 body: "requests per minute (RPM): Limit 30, Used 30". Docs agree. **But** a burst of 35 concurrent calls got 34 through; only 1 was refused. | Value high; enforcement under concurrency low (one burst) |
| Tokens per minute | 8,000 | `x-ratelimit-limit-tokens: 8000`; 429 body "Limit 8000, Used 7659, Requested 1279". 8 concurrent ~1.28K-token calls: 6 ok, 2 refused, exactly as the arithmetic predicts. | High |
| Requests per day | 1,000 | `x-ratelimit-limit-requests: 1000`. `reset-requests` grows by 86.4 s per call (= 86400/1000): a bucket refilling one request every 86.4 s, not a midnight reset. | High (value), medium (refill model) |
| Tokens per day | 200,000 (docs) | Docs only. No header carries it and I did not hit it. | Low: not measured |
| Requests in flight at once | No cap seen up to 35 | 35 concurrent calls all answered or refused for RPM, none for concurrency. | Low: only tested to 35 |
| What it returns when a limit is hit | HTTP 429, `retry-after` in whole seconds, JSON `{"error":{"message":…,"type":"requests"\|"tokens","code":"rate_limit_exceeded"}}`; message names the limit, used, requested, and a precise wait ("7.034999999s"). Refusal is fast: 62–237 ms. | Captured bodies in `calls.jsonl` | High |
| Time until it recovers | RPM: `retry-after: 2`, next poll 2 s later succeeded. TPM: depends on request size; tokens refill continuously at 8000/60 ≈ 133/s. The 1,279-token request was told 7.03 s = (1279 − 341 free) / 133.3. | Poll after 429; arithmetic on the 429 body | RPM medium; TPM medium (my recovery poll used a small request, which fit at once, so this is derived, not observed) |

## Latency (ok calls only)

| Phase | n | First token p50 / max (ms) | Total p50 / max (ms) | Tokens in / out (median) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| seq (small, one at a time) | 10 | 358 / 432 | 359 / 434 | 84 / 16 |
| big (~1.2K-token prompt, one at a time) | 5 | 416 / 680 | 482 / 743 | 1220 / 59 |
| tpm (big, 8 at once) | 6 | 506 / 1261 | 590 / 1285 | 1220 / 59 |
| rpm (tiny, 35 at once) | 34 | no content (see below) | 1215 / 1289 | 74 / 16 |

Fast when idle; total time roughly 3.5× when 35 arrive together. 61 calls cannot support a percentile beyond the median per phase.

## Findings that change the build

1. **TPM and RPD behave as token buckets, not fixed windows.** Header `x-ratelimit-reset-tokens` on the 429 was 57.4 s = time to refill to full at 133/s. The limiter should mirror that.
2. **The provider's RPM check leaked under a simultaneous burst** (34 of 35 passed against a limit of 30). The counters look eventually consistent. Our own limiter, not the provider, has to keep us inside the limit.
3. **A 200 OK can carry an empty answer.** All 34 `rpm` calls (`max_completion_tokens: 16`) spent every token on hidden reasoning and returned no content. The draft step must leave room for reasoning, and an empty draft must be treated as a failure.
4. **Remaining-tokens headers disagree with each other inside a burst** (values jump between 5,215 and 7,910 for calls finishing in the same millisecond). Header correction (good-to-have #1) must take the minimum seen in a short window, not the latest value.
5. **TPM binds first.** At ~1.3–2K tokens per answer, 8K TPM allows ~4–6 answers a minute, well under 30 RPM.

## Not yet clear

- Whether TPM admission counts `max_completion_tokens`. The smoke call's drop (106 = 74 prompt + 32 max) suggested yes; the 429 bodies ("Requested 1279" and "1282" for identical 1,220-token prompts with max 300) suggest Groq counts an estimate near prompt + actual, not the max. I treat it as **not counting max**, medium confidence.

## D6 — 2026-11-12 — Probe findings that change the design

**Finding:** TPM refills continuously (≈133 tokens/s) and RPD refills one request per 86.4 s; neither is a fixed window. Groq let 34 of 35 simultaneous calls through a 30 RPM limit. Remaining-tokens headers disagree within a burst. Details: `results/probe/README.md`.
**Decision:** (a) The limiter models token buckets, replacing DESIGN §5's sliding windows; final shape is decided when the limiter is written. (b) Our limiter is the real guard; provider 429s are a fallback. (c) Header correction trusts the lowest remaining value seen recently, never just the latest.
**Cost:** The "daily budget exhausted" scenario is not a cliff on the real service: one request trickles back every 86.4 s. The stand-in must model that refill too, or the L3 results will look worse than reality.

## D7 — 2026-11-12 — Empty answers are failures; reasoning needs headroom

**Finding:** With `max_completion_tokens: 16`, every call returned 200 OK with no content: hidden reasoning used the whole budget.
**Decision:** The draft call gets enough `max_completion_tokens` for reasoning plus answer (set from the eval). An empty draft fails verification like any other bad draft.
**Cost:** A larger max output, which matters if TPM admission counts it (open question in the probe README).
EOF

**Decision:** `Search` returns both the raw score and `Norm` = score / (Σ over query terms of idf·(k1+1)), the best score that query could ever get. T is compared with the top hit's `Norm`, not its raw score.

## D12 — 2026-11-12 — Admission estimates the wait from the limiter, queue included

**Decision:** On arrival, admission asks the limiter how long until this request *and every request queued ahead of it* fit the buckets, adds an expected service time, and takes the best rung that finishes before the person's deadline: L0 if the full answer fits, L1 if only the lighter one does, L2 ("busy, try in N s", N from the limiter, which includes the provider's retry hint) otherwise. When the binding limit is a daily one, L3 (retrieval only). One FIFO queue; a request whose deadline passes while queued leaves at that moment. Concurrency is not capped separately: the probe found no in-flight limit up to 35.
**Why:** TPM binds first (D6), so the token buckets, not a guessed service rate, set throughput. Not queueing what would time out keeps the queue made only of people who will still be there.
**Found while testing:** the queue-wide estimate can exceed one bucket's capacity. A per-request "never fits" check there would have sent long-queue requests to L3 as if the daily budget were gone. Queue estimates now use an uncapped refill time; "never fits" applies only to a single request.
**Cost:** A large request at the head blocks smaller ones behind it (FIFO by design, no priorities). Service time is a fixed guess until the runs measure it.
EOF

Decide estimates the wait for a request plus everyone queued ahead from
the limiter and picks L0, L1, L2 or L3 against the person's deadline.
Acquire waits in one FIFO queue served by a dispatcher; a request that
gives up leaves at once and returns any room granted in that instant.
Queue-wide estimates use an uncapped bucket refill time so a long queue
is a wait, not a never-fits." && git log --oneline | head -8

Phase 5 is the wiring. **Rewrite → retrieve → decide → admission → draft (with retries) → verify (with at most one redraft) → reply.** It needs four files:

- `rewrite.go`: drop question filler words.
- `prompt.go`: the model's rules, and the `[id] text` chunk format the stand-in already expects.
- `pipeline.go`: `Answer`, the one function that uses all five core files.
- `cmd/relay`: a command-line tool for asking a single question.

Two choices to flag now:

1. **What status do L2 and L3 get in `results.csv`?** Both are recorded as `rate_limited`, with `ladder_level` telling them apart. An L3 reply is useful, but it isn't a model answer, and a limit is the reason. Calling it `ok` would make the "budget exhausted" row of Table 2b look perfect when it isn't.
2. **What counts as "first token" for the person?** The reply is held back until it passes verify (DESIGN §2), so the first token the person sees arrives with the full reply. I record the model's own first token separately, for the "where the time goes" heading.

## D13 — 2026-11-12 — Pipeline wiring, and what the first real answers changed in verify

**Decisions:**
- Every model attempt, retries included, waits in the admission queue and holds a limiter reservation. After each attempt the pipeline settles the reservation, corrects the limiter from headers, and on a 429 pauses everyone for the retry hint.
- Provider limits are believed only from real headers. A failed call has none, and its zero-value limits once read as "0 requests left today", sending every later request to L3 (caught by a test that took 10 s instead of milliseconds; the client now marks limits unknown until headers arrive).
- `results.csv` status: L2 ("busy") and L3 (passages only) are `rate_limited`, distinguished by `ladder_level`. An L3 reply is useful but is not a model answer, and a limit is why.
- First token as the person sees it = release time (answers are buffered until verified, DESIGN §2). The model's own first token is kept separately for "where the time goes".
- Verify now also requires a citation in every sentence of 4+ words (D11 amended). The first real Groq answer contained an uncited sentence from the model's own knowledge that passed the old checks. Rather than refuse the whole answer, the pipeline **drops uncited sentences** and verifies what is left: the person gets less, never an unbacked claim.
- Quotes are compared case-insensitively, and a quote joining passages with "…" is checked piece by piece. Real Groq answers lowercased a quote's first word and joined two passages with an ellipsis; both are normal quoting and do not change what the source says.

**Cost:** Dropping sentences can leave a terse answer of quotes. Case-insensitive matching is slightly looser than "word for word". These were tuned on three real answers; the eval measures the false-refusal rate properly.
EOF

content.text:
Phase 8 is the load generator. Here's the plan, following DESIGN §6:

- **Open loop.** Requests start at their scheduled times whether or not earlier ones have finished. Latency is measured from the scheduled start, so a slow system can't hide behind a slow generator.
- **Lag check.** Every row records how late its start actually was (good-to-have #2).
- **Scenarios** are defined in code: arrival rates, how the stand-in behaves, what our limiter believes, and which retry policy is used.
- **Eval mode** runs the questions one at a time and grades each answer.

Two scenario decisions, both driven by the probe:

1. **Rates are set by TPM, not RPM.** At about 1.9K tokens per answer, 8K TPM allows roughly **4 answers a minute**. So "steady" means 3 per minute, and "overload" means 12 per minute (3× capacity).
2. **"Per-minute limit halved" halves the *provider* without telling our limiter.** The brief says limits "can change without notice". Our limiter still believes 8K TPM, and only learns the truth from Groq's headers and 429s. That's also where the naive retry policy can do real damage, which makes the comparison meaningful.

## D14 — 2026-11-12 — Load generator and scenarios

**Decisions:**
- Arrivals are a seeded Poisson process per phase (exponential gaps), not evenly spaced: real traffic is bursty even at a steady average. Bursts are N requests at one instant.
- Open loop: each request starts at its scheduled time in its own goroutine; latency runs from the scheduled start; every row records `start_lag_ms` (good-to-have #2, an extra column after the brief's).
- Rates follow the probe: TPM binds at ~4 answers/minute, so steady = 3/min, overload = 12/min. Burst = steady plus 20 at once at 1:00. "Halved" halves the stand-in's RPM/TPM *without telling our limiter*, which must learn from headers and 429s. "Daily-exhausted" starts the stand-in's RPD at 0 with the 86.4 s trickle.
- The naive-retry run is any scenario with `-policy naive`, so the comparison holds arrivals, seed and provider fixed. The naive policy also skips the limiter-wide pause on a 429 (otherwise our limiter would quietly make it polite).
- Eval runs the questions closed loop, one at a time, so Table 3 latencies are the pipeline's, not a queue's. Grading: every key phrase present and a citation from the expected paper.
- Only `eval` and `steady` may run against real Groq; the rest are refused on `-source real` to protect the shared daily budget.
- First token for timeouts/errors is empty: the person saw no answer.

"""Print the brief's results tables from results.csv, and nothing else.

Usage: python3 scripts/tables.py [results/results.csv]

Every number here is computed from that one file, so a reviewer can
recompute it. Percentiles are nearest-rank. Times in ms, percentages to
one decimal. "not measured" where a cell has no rows behind it.
"""

import csv
import math
import sys
from collections import defaultdict

NM = "not measured"


def pct(values, p):
    """Nearest-rank percentile: the smallest value with at least p% of
    values at or below it. None for an empty list."""
    if not values:
        return None
    s = sorted(values)
    rank = max(1, math.ceil(p / 100 * len(s)))
    return s[rank - 1]


def ms(v):
    return NM if v is None else str(int(v))


def triple(values, ps=(50, 95, 99)):
    if not values:
        return NM
    return " / ".join(ms(pct(values, p)) for p in ps)


def share(n, total):
    return NM if total == 0 else f"{100 * n / total:.1f}"


def num(row, col):
    v = row.get(col, "")
    return None if v == "" else float(v)


def load(path):
    with open(path, newline="") as f:
        return list(csv.DictReader(f))


def by(rows, key):
    groups = defaultdict(list)
    for r in rows:
        groups[key(r)].append(r)
    return dict(sorted(groups.items()))


def duration_s(rows):
    """Span of scheduled starts: how long the load was offered."""
    from datetime import datetime
    ts = [datetime.fromisoformat(r["start_time"].replace("Z", "+00:00")) for r in rows]
    return (max(ts) - min(ts)).total_seconds()


def table_2a(rows):
    out = ["| Scenario | Real or stand-in | Requests sent | Duration (s) | Offered rate (per min) | First token p50 / p95 / p99 (ms) | Total time p50 / p95 / p99 (ms) |",
           "|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|"]
    for (scen, src), rs in by(rows, lambda r: (r["scenario"], r["source"])).items():
        d = duration_s(rs)
        rate = NM if d == 0 else f"{60 * len(rs) / d:.1f}"
        first = [num(r, "first_token_ms") for r in rs if num(r, "first_token_ms") is not None]
        total = [num(r, "total_ms") for r in rs]
        out.append(f"| {scen} | {src} | {len(rs)} | {d:.0f} | {rate} | {triple(first)} | {triple(total)} |")
    return out


def answered(r):
    """A model answer was produced and shown (not a refusal, L2 or L3)."""
    return r["status"] == "ok" and int(num(r, "tokens_out") or 0) > 0


def table_2b(rows):
    out = ["| Scenario | Succeeded % | Rate-limited % | Timed out or given up % | Retries per request | Peak queue length | Tokens per answer | Cost per 1,000 answers |",
           "|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|"]
    for (scen, src), rs in by(rows, lambda r: (r["scenario"], r["source"])).items():
        n = len(rs)
        status = defaultdict(int)
        for r in rs:
            status[r["status"]] += 1
        retries = sum(num(r, "retries") or 0 for r in rs) / n
        peak = max(int(num(r, "queue_len_at_arrival") or 0) for r in rs)
        ans = [r for r in rs if answered(r)]
        tokens = NM if not ans else f"{sum(num(r, 'tokens_in') + num(r, 'tokens_out') for r in ans) / len(ans):.0f}"
        out.append(f"| {scen} ({src}) | {share(status['ok'], n)} | {share(status['rate_limited'], n)} | "
                   f"{share(status['timeout'], n)} | {retries:.2f} | {peak} | {tokens} | $0 (free tier) |")
    return out


def table_3(rows):
    out = ["| Setting | Questions asked | Correct and cited % | Wrong % | Correctly refused % | Tokens per answer | First token p50 / p95 (ms) | Total time p50 / p95 (ms) |",
           "|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|"]
    evals = [r for r in rows if r["answer_grade"]]
    for setting, rs in by(evals, lambda r: r["retrieval_setting"]).items():
        n = len(rs)
        g = defaultdict(int)
        for r in rs:
            g[r["answer_grade"]] += 1
        ans = [r for r in rs if answered(r)]
        tokens = NM if not ans else f"{sum(num(r, 'tokens_in') + num(r, 'tokens_out') for r in ans) / len(ans):.0f}"
        first = [num(r, "first_token_ms") for r in rs if num(r, "first_token_ms") is not None]
        total = [num(r, "total_ms") for r in rs]
        out.append(f"| {setting} | {n} | {share(g['correct'], n)} | {share(g['wrong'], n)} | {share(g['refused_correctly'], n)} | "
                   f"{tokens} | {triple(first, (50, 95))} | {triple(total, (50, 95))} |")
    return out


def slowest(rows):
    """Where the time goes: the slowest request per scenario, split into
    waiting (queue), working (model) and the rest (retries' backoff and
    our own overhead)."""
    out = ["| Scenario | Request | Total (ms) | Queue wait (ms) | Model (ms) | Other: backoff + overhead (ms) | Retries | Status |",
           "|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|"]
    for scen, rs in by(rows, lambda r: r["scenario"]).items():
        r = max(rs, key=lambda r: num(r, "total_ms"))
        total, queue, model = (num(r, c) for c in ("total_ms", "queue_wait_ms", "model_ms"))
        out.append(f"| {scen} | {r['request_id']} | {total:.0f} | {queue:.0f} | {model:.0f} | {total - queue - model:.0f} | {r['retries']} | {r['status']} |")
    return out


def main(path="results/results.csv"):
    rows = load(path)
    load_rows = [r for r in rows if not r["answer_grade"]]
    for title, lines in [("Table 2a: Latency per load scenario", table_2a(load_rows)),
                         ("Table 2b: Outcomes per load scenario", table_2b(load_rows)),
                         ("Table 3: Retrieval settings (graded eval rows)", table_3(rows)),
                         ("Where the time goes: slowest request per scenario", slowest(rows))]:
        print(f"\n### {title}\n")
        print("\n".join(lines))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main(*sys.argv[1:2])

import unittest

from tables import answered, pct, table_2b, table_3, triple


def row(**kw):
    base = {"request_id": "r", "scenario": "s", "source": "stand-in", "start_time": "2026-11-12T10:00:00Z",
            "first_token_ms": "100", "total_ms": "100", "status": "ok", "retries": "0", "tokens_in": "1000",
            "tokens_out": "100", "retrieval_setting": "R2", "answer_grade": "", "queue_len_at_arrival": "0",
            "queue_wait_ms": "0", "model_ms": "90"}
    base.update(kw)
    return base


class Percentile(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_nearest_rank(self):
        xs = [15, 20, 35, 40, 50]
        self.assertEqual(pct(xs, 50), 35)
        self.assertEqual(pct(xs, 95), 50)
        self.assertEqual(pct(xs, 1), 15)
        self.assertIsNone(pct([], 50))

    def test_triple_not_measured(self):
        self.assertEqual(triple([]), "not measured")


class Tables(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_2b_counts_and_tokens_only_over_answers(self):
        rows = [row(), row(status="rate_limited", tokens_in="0", tokens_out="0", queue_len_at_arrival="7"),
                row(status="timeout", retries="2", tokens_in="0", tokens_out="0"), row(tokens_out="0", tokens_in="0")]
        line = table_2b(rows)[2]
        # 3 of 4... no: statuses are ok, rate_limited, timeout, ok -> 50% ok.
        self.assertIn("| s (stand-in) | 50.0 | 25.0 | 25.0 | 0.50 | 7 | 1100 |", line)

    def test_answered_excludes_refusals(self):
        self.assertTrue(answered(row()))
        self.assertFalse(answered(row(tokens_out="0")))
        self.assertFalse(answered(row(status="rate_limited")))

    def test_3_grades(self):
        rows = [row(answer_grade="correct"), row(answer_grade="wrong"),
                row(answer_grade="refused_correctly", tokens_out="0"), row(answer_grade="refused_wrongly", tokens_out="0")]
        self.assertIn("| R2 | 4 | 25.0 | 25.0 | 25.0 | 1100 |", table_3(rows)[2])


if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()

"""Choose the refusal threshold T from a T=0 eval run on the dev half.

Usage: python3 scripts/tune_t.py results/results.csv eval/questions.json

With T=0 every question reached the model, and each row recorded its
top_norm. A threshold T would have refused, without a model call, every
question whose top_norm < T. This replays that for a grid of T values:
no extra calls are needed to compare thresholds.
"""

import csv
import json
import sys
from collections import defaultdict


def replay(rows, t):
    """Grades as they would be under threshold t."""
    out = []
    for r in rows:
        if float(r["top_norm"]) < t:
            out.append("refused_wrongly" if r["_answerable"] else "refused_correctly")
        else:
            out.append(r["answer_grade"])
    return out


def main(results_path, questions_path, split="dev"):
    questions = {q["id"]: q for q in json.load(open(questions_path))}
    rows = [r for r in csv.DictReader(open(results_path, newline=""))
            if r["scenario"] == "eval" and r["question_id"] in questions
            and questions[r["question_id"]]["split"] == split]
    for r in rows:
        r["_answerable"] = questions[r["question_id"]]["answerable"]

    grid = [round(0.05 * i, 2) for i in range(0, 11)]
    for setting, rs in sorted(_group(rows).items()):
        print(f"\n{setting} ({len(rs)} {split} questions)")
        print("   T    correct  wrong  refused_ok  refused_wrongly")
        for t in grid:
            g = defaultdict(int)
            for grade in replay(rs, t):
                g[grade] += 1
            print(f"  {t:.2f}  {g['correct']:7d}  {g['wrong']:5d}  {g['refused_correctly']:10d}  {g['refused_wrongly']:15d}")

input.content:
# The Relay

A Go pipeline that answers questions about three arXiv papers with verified citations, a traffic controller that keeps it inside Groq's free-tier limits, and a small lab to test it: a stand-in model server, an open-loop load generator, and a recorder that writes `results/results.csv`.

One rule drives every choice: **under pressure the Relay gives less, never something wrong.**

Design: [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md). Every change since, with its cost: [DECISIONS.md](DECISIONS.md). Probe findings and Table 1: [results/probe/README.md](results/probe/README.md).

## Requirements

- Go 1.27+, Python 3, `pdftotext` (poppler)
- `GROQ_API_KEY` in the environment, only for real runs. Tests never call Groq.

## Layout

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| `internal/retrieve` | Tokenizer and BM25 (own implementation) |
| `internal/pipeline` | Rewrite → retrieve → decide → draft → verify; `verify.go` is the "never wrong" check |
| `internal/traffic` | Limiter (token buckets), retry policy, admission queue + degradation ladder |
| `internal/llm` | Streaming client for any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, typed errors |
| `internal/standin` | Fake provider calibrated from the probe |
| `internal/loadgen`, `cmd/loadgen` | Open-loop load generator, scenarios, graded eval |
| `internal/corpus`, `scripts/parse.py` | PDF → page/section-tagged text → chunks |
| `cmd/probe` | Planned real calls that measured the limits |
| `scripts/tables.py` | Every results table, from `results/results.csv` only |

## Reproduce

```bash
make hooks && make check                       # gofmt, vet, tests (+race), Python tests
./scripts/fetch.sh && python3 scripts/parse.py data/pdf data/parsed
go run ./cmd/relay -q "Why does the Transformer scale dot products?"     # one real question
go run ./cmd/loadgen -scenario burst                                     # stand-in load run
go run ./cmd/loadgen -scenario halved -policy naive                      # naive-retry comparison
go run ./cmd/loadgen -scenario eval -source real -split heldout          # graded real eval
python3 scripts/tables.py results/results.csv
```

Scenarios: `steady`, `burst`, `overload`, `halved` (provider limits halved without notice), `daily-exhausted`, each optionally with `-policy naive`. Only `eval` and `steady` may run against real Groq, to protect the shared daily budget.

## Status

`eval/questions.json` currently holds **placeholder** questions (`author: placeholder`); graded results from them are for building and tuning only.

## D16 — 2026-11-12 — Fixes found by the Phase 9 runs, and what was re-run

**Bugs the runs exposed (each fixed with a regression test that fails on the old code):**
1. *Verify refused correct quotes over one character.* The model writes U+2011 (non-breaking hyphen) in "Mamba‑2", "self‑supervised", "H‑Net"; the papers use plain hyphens. All three `refused_wrongly` rows of the first held-out run were correct answers. Every Unicode hyphen and dash now normalises to "-".
2. *A 429 pause hid the daily limit.* In the daily-exhausted run Groq-shaped 87 s retry hints outlasted the 86.4 s day refill, the limiter named the pause as the reason, and two people got L2 "busy" instead of L3 passages. A blocking day limit is now always the reason.
3. *Request ids were not unique.* The eval loop starts one run per question and ids restarted at 0000; two questions in the same second shared an id. Ids now use a process-wide counter.

**Data handling (no measured value changed):** the first held-out run and the buggy daily-exhausted run are moved to `results/buggy/` as superseded. **Caveat:** bug 1 was found by reading held-out failures, so the re-run held-out half is no longer fully untouched by tuning. The fix is general (Unicode normalisation), not fitted to those questions.
EOF

# The Relay — write-up

> **DRAFT.** Sections marked **[YOU: …]** need your own words. Graded results use the 20 **placeholder** questions (`author: placeholder`); replace them and re-run `eval` before submitting. Every number here is recomputable with `python3 scripts/tables.py results/results.csv`.

## 1. What I built and why

A Go pipeline over the three papers: **rewrite** (rules) → **retrieve** (own BM25, the tool call) → **decide** (refuse with no model call if the best normalised score < T) → **draft** (one Groq call, `gpt-oss-20b`) → **verify** (string checks, at most one redraft). In front of the model sits a traffic controller: token-bucket **limiter**, **retry** policy, one FIFO **admission** queue and a four-rung **ladder** (L0 full, L1 fewer chunks/no redraft, L2 "busy, try in N s", L3 cited passages with no model call).

**The decision that shaped it most: under pressure the Relay gives less, never something wrong.** Answers are buffered until verified: every sentence must carry a chunk id, cited ids must have been retrieved, every quote must appear in its chunk word for word (after typography normalisation), and at least one 3+ word quote must back the answer. Uncited sentences are deleted, not shown. I gave up time-to-first-token for this: the person's first token *is* the whole verified answer.

## 2. The real service and my stand-in

I measured limits with 61 planned calls (`cmd/probe`, raw in `results/probe/`), not from memory:

| Limit | Value found | How I found it | Confidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Requests per minute | 30 | 429 body "RPM: Limit 30, Used 30"; docs agree. A burst of 35 got 34 through | Value high; enforcement low |
| Tokens per minute | 8,000 | `x-ratelimit-limit-tokens`; 8 concurrent 1.28K-token calls: 6 ok, 2 refused, as predicted | High |
| Requests per day | 1,000 | `x-ratelimit-limit-requests`; `reset-requests` grows 86.4 s per call: refills one per 86.4 s | High |
| Tokens per day | 200,000 | Docs only; no header | Low: not measured |
| Requests in flight at once | No cap seen up to 35 | 35 concurrent calls | Low |
| What it returns when a limit is hit | HTTP 429, `retry-after` in whole seconds, JSON naming the limit and a precise wait; in 62–237 ms | Captured bodies | High |
| Time until it recovers | RPM 2 s; TPM = shortfall ÷ 133 tokens/s (7.03 s for a 1,279-token call) | Poll after 429; 429-body arithmetic | Medium |

**Stand-in** (`internal/standin`, same wire format, so the client cannot tell): first-token delay resampled from the probe, +0.05 ms per prompt token, +24 ms per other request in flight (a line through two bursts), 0.8 ms per output token; token-bucket limits with Groq-shaped headers and 429 bodies; 20 hidden reasoning tokens, so a tiny `max_tokens` returns an empty 200 exactly as Groq did; injectable 5xx and dropped connections. **Least like the real thing:** real slowness comes from other tenants, not my load; my limits are exact where Groq leaked 34 of 35; failure rates are chosen (the probe saw none, yet the real steady run then saw 1 timeout and 2 dropped connections in 16).

## 3. Results

Real = Groq free tier; stand-in = calibrated fake. "First token" is when the verified reply is released.

## 4. Where the time goes

Real steady `steady-R1-071824-0005`: 12,274 ms = **11,868 waiting** for TPM in our queue + **400 working** in the model + 6 ours, no retries; all before the first token. Measured around `Acquire` and `Complete` per row.

## 5. When a limit is hit

**Per minute:** our limiter holds requests. Admission estimates the wait for a request *plus everyone queued ahead* and gives the best rung that finishes in the person's 20 s: L0, else L1, else L2 at once. Burst: 17 L0, 1 L1, 14 L2, no timeouts, no provider 429s. Only someone whose deadline passes in the queue is dropped, at that moment. **Per day:** new requests get L3; running ones finish.

## Retrieval: quality versus cost

| Setting (piece size, pieces, re-rank) | Questions asked | Correct and cited % | Wrong % | Correctly refused % | Tokens per answer | First token p50 / p95 (ms) | Total time p50 / p95 (ms) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| R1: 150 words, 6, no (dev) | 10 | 40.0 | 20.0 | 30.0 | 1999 | 12243 / 21768 | 12243 / 21768 |
| R2: 300 words, 4, no (dev) | 10 | 40.0 | 20.0 | 30.0 | 2438 | 16156 / 32763 | 16156 / 32763 |
| R3: 300 words, 2, no (dev) | 10 | 20.0 | 30.0 | 30.0 | 1785 | 9311 / 24583 | 9311 / 24583 |
| R1 (held-out, chosen) | 10 | 40.0 | 40.0 | 20.0 | 2012 | 9095 / 25718 | 9095 / 25718 |

**R1:** R2's quality with 18% fewer tokens, and tokens per minute binds. Latency is mostly TPM queueing. Near the limit, L1 uses 2 chunks; at L3 retrieval is the answer. T = 0.13 only saves tokens: the model refused every unanswerable dev question itself.

## How this library will mislead a naive retriever

1. **Shared vocabulary.** "H-Net's latency in real-time spoken dialogue?" pulled Moshi chunks; the model answered "160ms" citing Moshi, and verify passed the real quote.
2. **Table-only facts.** "Parameters of the big Transformer?": 213M is in Table 3, flattened to unlabelled numbers; the model refused.
3. **Page furniture.** Moshi's title on every page makes "What is Moshi?" match every chunk; we strip repeated lines.

## 6. Retries

Only 429, 5xx, timeouts, dropped connections; ≤2; the provider's hint plus jitter, else full-jitter backoff; never past the deadline. **Worse:** with limits silently halved, naive retries (fixed 1 s, hint ignored) hit 3 429s instead of 1 on `…-0011` and still failed, 11.8 s vs 9.5 s. Small: under plain overload both tied, as our limiter kept calls off Groq's 429s.

## 7. What the person sees

In ~20 ms, zero tokens: *"Our daily model budget is used up, so I can't write an answer. These passages from the papers best match your question:"* and three cited excerpts. Never wrong; may not answer. One request returns every 86.4 s.

## 8. What I'm unsure about, what I left out, what I learned

The probe showed `x-ratelimit-reset-requests` growing by 86.4 s with every call: 86,400 s ÷ 1,000. The allowance refills continuously, so "daily budget exhausted" is not a cliff: one request comes back every 86.4 s, and both the limiter and the stand-in had to be built around that.

## Your feedback on Vaani

I have followed Vaani's journey for about a year, since I first reached out to Tushar; his work has inspired me since. With Vaani's launch as a product I enjoyed going through the docs: the number of features is remarkable. Two stood out: interruption handling, which was new to me, and adding ambient background sound. **[YOU: one thing that confused you, and one thing you would change.]**

## How I worked with the assistant

I started by sitting with Claude to understand what we were building, then did the system design myself and wrote `DESIGN.md`, where every decision was taken after careful consideration. With the build plan ready, building it was a matter of time. I hold one rule: never ship a line of code I don't understand. AI is good when it raises your speed and efficiency, not when it makes your decisions, and that is where I spent most of my effort in this project: the design and architecture. Most of the code was produced by Claude, but I went through every file, and from the very beginning every file and function has its own tests; each new feature ran the full suite (`gofmt`, `go vet`, tests with the race detector) before its commit, so we never broke something or faked it.

**Prompts that mattered:** giving it my design with one rule, *give less, never something wrong*; "run the probe", which turned assumed limits into measured ones; and "fix and rerun", which found three more bugs instead of shipping the first numbers. **Caught:** verify let an uncited sentence from the model's own knowledge through; all tests passed, and I caught it on the first real Groq answer. Later its first fix for a "busy instead of passages" bug was not the cause; a test reproducing the run found the real one. **Overruled:** it recommended writing my own questions before any eval; I chose to run with placeholders to keep moving, and the graded runs had to be redone. **Distinctly mine:** the one-rule design, a single model call with rule-based rewriting, the zero-token L3 rung, the open-loop generator with its lag check, and measuring limits instead of trusting the docs.

# The Relay — write-up

> **DRAFT.** **[YOU: …]** marks your own words. Graded rows use 20 **placeholder** questions; replace and re-run `eval` first. Numbers: `python3 scripts/tables.py results/results.csv`; reasons and costs: `DECISIONS.md`.

## 1. What I built and why

Go pipeline: **rewrite** (rules) → **retrieve** (own BM25) → **decide** (refuse with no model call if top normalised score < T) → **draft** (one Groq call) → **verify** (string checks, ≤1 redraft), behind a token-bucket limiter, a retry policy, one FIFO queue and a ladder: L0 full, L1 fewer chunks, L2 "busy, try in N s", L3 cited passages, no model call. **Deciding choice: under pressure give less, never something wrong.** Replies are held until every sentence cites a retrieved chunk and every quote is in its chunk word for word; uncited sentences are deleted. Cost: the first token *is* the whole answer.

## 2. The real service and my stand-in

| Limit | Value found | How found | Confidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Requests per minute | 30 | 429 body; yet 34 of a 35-call burst passed | Value high; enforcement low |
| Tokens per minute | 8,000 | header; 8 concurrent 1.28K-token calls: 6 ok, 2 refused | High |
| Requests per day | 1,000 | header; reset grows 86.4 s per call (refill, not midnight) | High |
| Tokens per day | 200,000 | docs only | Low: not measured |
| Requests in flight | no cap up to 35 | 35 concurrent calls | Low |
| When a limit is hit | 429 in 62–237 ms; `retry-after`; body names limit and wait | captured | High |
| Time to recover | RPM 2 s; TPM shortfall ÷ 133 tokens/s | poll; arithmetic on 429 | Medium |

From 61 planned calls (`results/probe/`). The **stand-in** speaks Groq's wire format, resamples first-token delay from the probe, adds 24 ms per other request in flight, and refuses with Groq-shaped buckets, headers and 429s. **Least like Groq:** real slowness comes from other tenants, not my load; its limits are exact where Groq leaked; its failures are chosen, while real steady saw 3 in 16.

## 3. Results

| Scenario | Real or stand-in | Requests sent | Duration (s) | Offered rate (per min) | First token p50 / p95 / p99 (ms) | Total time p50 / p95 / p99 (ms) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Steady | real | 16 | 268 | 3.6 | 2171 / 12274 / 12274 | 2171 / 12274 / 12274 |
| Burst (20 at once) | stand-in | 32 | 199 | 9.7 | 15 / 7479 / 7605 | 15 / 7479 / 7605 |
| Sustained overload | stand-in | 48 | 221 | 13.0 | 523 / 15175 / 19286 | 523 / 17585 / 20001 |
| Per-minute limit halved | stand-in | 12 | 199 | 3.6 | 450 / 9530 / 9530 | 450 / 9530 / 9530 |
| Daily budget exhausted | stand-in | 7 | 148 | 2.8 | 18 / 547 / 547 | 18 / 547 / 547 |

| Scenario | Succeeded % | Rate-limited % | Timed out or given up % | Retries per request | Peak queue length | Tokens per answer | Cost per 1,000 answers (list price) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Steady (real) | 81.2 | 0.0 | 6.2 | 0.44 | 0 | 2466 | $0.218 |
| Burst | 56.2 | 43.8 | 0.0 | 0.00 | 2 | 1396 | $0.115 |
| Sustained overload | 70.8 | 27.1 | 2.1 | 0.04 | 3 | 1193 | $0.099 |
| Limit halved | 91.7 | 8.3 | 0.0 | 0.00 | 0 | 1424 | $0.117 |
| Daily budget exhausted | 28.6 | 71.4 | 0.0 | 0.00 | 0 | 1380 | $0.114 |

Cost is $0 on the free tier; shown at $0.075/$0.30 per M tokens in/out. Real steady's other 12.5% are dropped connections; rate-limited includes L2/L3. The stand-in's steady run: p50 448 ms, 100% ok. **Quality** (held-out, 10): 40% correct and cited, 40% wrong, 20% correctly refused, 2,012 tokens/answer; by hand 6 correct, 1 wrong (`results/eval_review.md`). **Unguessable:** 34 of 35 passed a 30 RPM limit; three correct answers were refused over U+2011 in "Mamba‑2".

## 4. Where the time goes

Real steady `steady-R1-071824-0005`: 12,274 ms = **11,868 waiting** in our queue for TPM + **400 working** in the model + 6 ours, no retries; all before the first token (per-row `queue_wait_ms`, `model_ms`).

## 5. When a limit is hit

**Per minute:** our limiter holds requests; admission estimates the wait for a request *plus everyone queued ahead* and gives the best rung that finishes in the person's 20 s (L0, else L1, else L2 at once). Burst: 17 L0, 1 L1, 14 L2, no timeouts, no provider 429s. Dropped: only someone whose deadline passes while queued. **Per day:** new requests get L3; running ones finish.

## Retrieval: quality versus cost

| Setting (piece size, pieces, re-rank) | Questions asked | Correct and cited % | Wrong % | Correctly refused % | Tokens per answer | First token p50 / p95 (ms) | Total time p50 / p95 (ms) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| R1: 150 words, 6, no (dev) | 10 | 40.0 | 20.0 | 30.0 | 1999 | 12243 / 21768 | 12243 / 21768 |
| R2: 300 words, 4, no (dev) | 10 | 40.0 | 20.0 | 30.0 | 2438 | 16156 / 32763 | 16156 / 32763 |
| R3: 300 words, 2, no (dev) | 10 | 20.0 | 30.0 | 30.0 | 1785 | 9311 / 24583 | 9311 / 24583 |
| R1 (held-out, chosen) | 10 | 40.0 | 40.0 | 20.0 | 2012 | 9095 / 25718 | 9095 / 25718 |

**R1:** R2's quality, 18% fewer tokens; tokens per minute binds. Latency is mostly TPM queueing. Near the limit L1 uses 2 chunks; at L3 retrieval is the answer. T = 0.13 only saves tokens: the model refused every unanswerable dev question.

## How this library will mislead a naive retriever

(1) **Shared vocabulary:** "H-Net's latency in real-time spoken dialogue?" pulled Moshi chunks; the model answered "160ms" citing Moshi, and verify passed the real quote. (2) **Table-only facts:** "Parameters of the big Transformer?": 213M sits in Table 3, flattened to unlabelled numbers; the model refused. (3) **Page furniture:** Moshi's title on every page makes "What is Moshi?" match every chunk; we strip repeated lines.

## 6. Retries

Only 429, 5xx, timeouts, dropped connections; ≤2; the provider's hint plus jitter, else full-jitter backoff; never past the deadline. **Worse:** with limits silently halved, naive retries (fixed 1 s, hint ignored) hit 3 429s instead of 1 on `…-0011` and still failed, 11.8 s vs 9.5 s. Small: under plain overload both tied, as our limiter kept calls off Groq's 429s.

## 7. What the person sees

In ~20 ms, zero tokens: *"Our daily model budget is used up, so I can't write an answer. These passages from the papers best match your question:"* plus three cited excerpts: never wrong, maybe not an answer. One request returns every 86.4 s.

## 8. What I'm unsure about, what I left out, what I learned

**Least certain:** 20 s patience; at 5 s most queued answers under load are lost and the ladder must step down earlier. **Not built:** a re-ranker; a check that a cited paper is the one the question names (would have refused q19). **[YOU: one thing new to you, in your words.]**

**[YOU: what stood out, what confused you, one change.]**

**[YOU: half a page; attach the real history.]**

The **stand-in** speaks Groq's wire format, resamples first-token delay from the probe, adds 24 ms per other request in flight, and refuses with Groq-shaped buckets, headers and 429s. **Least like Groq:** real slowness comes from other tenants, not my load; its limits are exact where Groq leaked; its failures are chosen, while real steady saw 3 in 16.

## 3. Results

| Scenario | Real or stand-in | Requests sent | Duration (s) | Offered rate (per min) | First token p50 / p95 / p99 (ms) | Total time p50 / p95 / p99 (ms) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Steady | real | 16 | 268 | 3.6 | 2171 / 12274 / 12274 | 2171 / 12274 / 12274 |
| Burst (20 at once) | stand-in | 32 | 199 | 9.7 | 15 / 7479 / 7605 | 15 / 7479 / 7605 |
| Sustained overload | stand-in | 48 | 221 | 13.0 | 523 / 15175 / 19286 | 523 / 17585 / 20001 |
| Per-minute limit halved | stand-in | 12 | 199 | 3.6 | 450 / 9530 / 9530 | 450 / 9530 / 9530 |
| Daily budget exhausted | stand-in | 7 | 148 | 2.8 | 18 / 547 / 547 | 18 / 547 / 547 |

| Scenario | Succeeded % | Rate-limited % | Timed out or given up % | Retries per request | Peak queue length | Tokens per answer | Cost per 1,000 answers (list price) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Steady (real) | 81.2 | 0.0 | 6.2 | 0.44 | 0 | 2466 | $0.218 |
| Burst | 56.2 | 43.8 | 0.0 | 0.00 | 2 | 1396 | $0.115 |
| Sustained overload | 70.8 | 27.1 | 2.1 | 0.04 | 3 | 1193 | $0.099 |
| Limit halved | 91.7 | 8.3 | 0.0 | 0.00 | 0 | 1424 | $0.117 |
| Daily budget exhausted | 28.6 | 71.4 | 0.0 | 0.00 | 0 | 1380 | $0.114 |

Cost is $0 on the free tier; shown at $0.075/$0.30 per M tokens in/out. Real steady's other 12.5% are dropped connections; rate-limited includes L2/L3. The stand-in's steady run: p50 448 ms, 100% ok. **Quality** (held-out, 10): 40% correct and cited, 40% wrong, 20% correctly refused, 2,012 tokens/answer; by hand 6 correct, 1 wrong (`results/eval_review.md`). **Unguessable:** 34 of 35 passed a 30 RPM limit; three correct answers were refused over U+2011 in "Mamba‑2".

## 4. Where the time goes

Real steady `steady-R1-071824-0005`: 12,274 ms = **11,868 waiting** in our queue for TPM + **400 working** in the model + 6 ours, no retries; all before the first token (per-row `queue_wait_ms`, `model_ms`).

## 5. When a limit is hit

**Per minute:** our limiter holds requests; admission estimates the wait for a request *plus everyone queued ahead* and gives the best rung that finishes in the person's 20 s (L0, else L1, else L2 at once). Burst: 17 L0, 1 L1, 14 L2, no timeouts, no provider 429s. Dropped: only someone whose deadline passes while queued. **Per day:** new requests get L3; running ones finish.

## Retrieval: quality versus cost

| Setting (piece size, pieces, re-rank) | Questions asked | Correct and cited % | Wrong % | Correctly refused % | Tokens per answer | First token p50 / p95 (ms) | Total time p50 / p95 (ms) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| R1: 150 words, 6, no (dev) | 10 | 40.0 | 20.0 | 30.0 | 1999 | 12243 / 21768 | 12243 / 21768 |
| R2: 300 words, 4, no (dev) | 10 | 40.0 | 20.0 | 30.0 | 2438 | 16156 / 32763 | 16156 / 32763 |
| R3: 300 words, 2, no (dev) | 10 | 20.0 | 30.0 | 30.0 | 1785 | 9311 / 24583 | 9311 / 24583 |
| R1 (held-out, chosen) | 10 | 40.0 | 40.0 | 20.0 | 2012 | 9095 / 25718 | 9095 / 25718 |

**R1:** R2's quality, 18% fewer tokens; tokens per minute binds. Latency is mostly TPM queueing. Near the limit L1 uses 2 chunks; at L3 retrieval is the answer. T = 0.13 only saves tokens: the model refused every unanswerable dev question.

## How this library will mislead a naive retriever

(1) **Shared vocabulary:** "H-Net's latency in real-time spoken dialogue?" pulled Moshi chunks; the model answered "160ms" citing Moshi, and verify passed the real quote. (2) **Table-only facts:** "Parameters of the big Transformer?": 213M sits in Table 3, flattened to unlabelled numbers; the model refused. (3) **Page furniture:** Moshi's title on every page makes "What is Moshi?" match every chunk; we strip repeated lines.

## 6. Retries

Only 429, 5xx, timeouts, dropped connections; ≤2; the provider's hint plus jitter, else full-jitter backoff; never past the deadline. **Worse:** with limits silently halved, naive retries (fixed 1 s, hint ignored) hit 3 429s instead of 1 on `…-0011` and still failed, 11.8 s vs 9.5 s. Small: under plain overload both tied, as our limiter kept calls off Groq's 429s.

## 7. What the person sees

In ~20 ms, zero tokens: *"Our daily model budget is used up, so I can't write an answer. These passages from the papers best match your question:"* plus three cited excerpts: never wrong, maybe not an answer. One request returns every 86.4 s.

## 8. What I'm unsure about, what I left out, what I learned

**Least certain:** 20 s patience; at 5 s most queued answers under load are lost and the ladder must step down earlier. **Not built:** a re-ranker; a check that a cited paper is the one the question names (would have refused q19). **New to me: rate limits are buckets that refill, not counters that reset.** I expected "1,000 requests per day" to reset at midnight. The probe showed `x-ratelimit-reset-requests` growing by 86.4 s with every call: 86,400 s ÷ 1,000. The allowance refills continuously, so "daily budget exhausted" is not a cliff: one request comes back every 86.4 s, and both the limiter and the stand-in had to be built around that.

## Your feedback on Vaani

I have followed Vaani's journey for about a year, since I first reached out to Tushar; his work has inspired me since. With Vaani's launch as a product I enjoyed going through the docs: the number of features is remarkable. Two stood out: interruption handling, which was new to me, and adding ambient background sound. **[YOU: one thing that confused you, and one thing you would change.]**

## How I worked with the assistant

I started by sitting with Claude to understand what we were building, then did the system design myself and wrote `DESIGN.md`, where every decision was taken after careful consideration. With the build plan ready, building it was a matter of time. I hold one rule: never ship a line of code I don't understand. AI is good when it raises your speed and efficiency, not when it makes your decisions, and that is where I spent most of my effort in this project: the design and architecture. Most of the code was produced by Claude, but I went through every file, and from the very beginning every file and function has its own tests; each new feature ran the full suite (`gofmt`, `go vet`, tests with the race detector) before its commit, so we never broke something or faked it.

**Prompts that mattered:** giving it my design with one rule, *give less, never something wrong*; "run the probe", which turned assumed limits into measured ones; and "fix and rerun", which found three more bugs instead of shipping the first numbers. **Caught:** verify let an uncited sentence from the model's own knowledge through; all tests passed, and I caught it on the first real Groq answer. Later its first fix for a "busy instead of passages" bug was not the cause; a test reproducing the run found the real one. **Overruled:** it recommended writing my own questions before any eval; I chose to run with placeholders to keep moving, and the graded runs had to be redone. **Distinctly mine:** the one-rule design, a single model call with rule-based rewriting, the zero-token L3 rung, the open-loop generator with its lag check, and measuring limits instead of trusting the docs.

## Your "what confused me", expanded

**Version A, for §8 (recommended).** "What I learned" is where it fits best, because the brief itself sets this tension up ("fast, good, cheap, nobody turned away; it cannot have all four"):

> **What I found hardest:** deciding what to optimise. The brief wants every reply fast, good, cheap and nobody turned away, and says plainly it cannot have all four. I could not build for all four, so the work was choosing a mix and a priority order: correctness first (never a wrong answer), then availability (always *some* reply, even passages at zero tokens), then cost (tokens per minute is the binding limit), and speed last (I accepted that the first token is the whole verified answer). Every rung of the ladder is that trade-off made explicit.

**Version B, if you want it in the Vaani section.** Then it has to be clearly about the *assignment*, so it doesn't read as confusion about Vaani's product:

> What challenged me most in the assignment was deciding what to prioritise among speed, quality, cost and availability, knowing all four can't be maximised together; finding the right mix was the real design work.

Version A is stronger: it shows your reasoning, and it explains why your ladder looks the way it does.

## "One thing I would change": pick one you actually agree with

1. **Publish rate limits and what happens at the limit.** *(Most "you", because it comes straight out of this project.)* The site gives a p90 latency of about 450ms but no plan limits. Building the Relay taught you how much a developer needs to know the per-minute and concurrency limits and what comes back when one is hit, such as a retry hint.
2. **Show latency as a distribution, and under load.** "p90 ~450ms" is good, but a p50/p99 figure and how it changes under many concurrent calls would say more. That's exactly what your Tables 2a/2b measure.
3. **One docs home and an overview page.** There are two docs domains (`docs.vaani.dev` and `docs.vaanivoice.ai`), and the docs open straight onto a backend REST API page. An overview of how a call flows (speech → model → voice, turn-taking, interruption) would help, and it connects to the interruption handling you liked.
4. **A clear developer path from the homepage.** There are two calls to action (sign up, or book an enterprise call), but no "build your first agent in 5 minutes" path and no SDK list.

> ## Documentation Index
> Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://docs.vaanivoice.ai/llms.txt
> Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.

# Quickstart

> Trigger your first outbound call and verify it works end-to-end

You've set up your account, created an agent, connected a phone number, and generated an API key. Now let's put it all together and make your first outbound call.

## Prerequisites

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Before you start:** Make sure you have these ready:
>
> * **A Vaani account** → [Create an Account](https://docs.vaanivoice.ai/getting-started/create-account.md)
> * **Your `agent_id` (UUID)** → [Create an Agent](https://docs.vaanivoice.ai/getting-started/create-agent.md)
> * **A connected phone number** → [Set Up Telephony](https://docs.vaanivoice.ai/getting-started/setup-telephony.md)
> * **Your API key** → [Generate an API Key](https://docs.vaanivoice.ai/getting-started/generate-api-key.md)

> [!NOTE]
>
> Have a personal phone handy to receive the test call. You'll use your own number as the `contact_number` so you can hear the agent in action.

## Trigger a Call

Replace `YOUR_API_KEY` and `YOUR_AGENT_ID` with your actual values, and set `contact_number` to the phone number you want to call (your own mobile is perfect for testing):

```bash cURL theme={null}
curl -X POST 'https://api.vaanivoice.ai/api/trigger-call/' \
  -H 'X-API-Key: YOUR_API_KEY' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "agent_id": "YOUR_AGENT_ID",
    "contact_number": "+919876543210",
    "name": "Test Call",
    "metadata": {}
  }'
```

```python Python theme={null}
import os
import requests

response = requests.post(
    "https://api.vaanivoice.ai/api/trigger-call/",
    headers={
        "X-API-Key": os.getenv("VAANI_API_KEY"),
        "Content-Type": "application/json"
    },
    json={
        "agent_id": "YOUR_AGENT_ID",
        "contact_number": "+919876543210",
        "name": "Test Call",
        "metadata": {}
    }
)

print(response.json())
```

## Request Fields Explained

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
| - | - | - | - |
| `agent_id` | string (UUID) | Yes | The agent to handle this call. Copy this from your Agent Config dashboard. |
| `contact_number` | string | Yes | The phone number to call, in E.164 format (e.g. `+919876543210`). `phone_number` is accepted as an alias. |

| `voice` | string | No | Override the agent's default voice for this specific call. Omit to use the voice configured on the agent. |

  "customer_name": "Rahul Sharma",
  "property_name": "Prateek Laurel"
}
